#110837. These 7 Porsches Have A Reputation For Being Nearly Indestructible

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1994 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

These 7 Porsches Have A Reputation For Being Nearly Indestructible

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for many, owning a Porsche is something of a dream.
  • It's models like the 996-generation 911 that might give buyers a reason to pause, as while the right advice could save 996 buyers from getting screwed, the model is still plagued with complex challenges.
  • Industry observers note that that need not end the dream for Porsche fans, though, as there is still a plethora of used Porsches that have proven pretty much indestructible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for many, owning a Porsche is something of a dream. However, keeping one running as it should year after year without having to spend thousands in preventative maintenance or labor-intensive repairs might not be all that easy. Sure, the automaker enjoys a reputation for engineering excellence, but that doesn't mean each model from its back catalog is as capable as the last when it comes to covering moon mileage.

It's models like the 996-generation 911 that might give buyers a reason to pause, as while the right advice could save 996 buyers from getting screwed, the model is still plagued with complex challenges. Problems such as failed intermediate shaft (IMS) bearings and cylinder bore scoring promptly make the 996 look less of a tempting proposition for those who need something they can rely upon.

Industry observers note that that need not end the dream for Porsche fans, though, as there is still a plethora of used Porsches that have proven pretty much indestructible. Some are cheap, like the 987.2-generation Boxster, and some are far from it, such as the iconic "widowmaker" 930 Turbo. What they all prove, however, is that with the correct maintenance and know-how, a secondhand Porsche really can run forever. Here are seven of our favorites, listed from the oldest through to the newest, and justified via high-mileage examples, owner reviews, and expert opinions.

In a recent development, it can be difficult to deduce whether the Porsche 924 was a success. It sold rather well, with a total of 152,082 finding homes across its full production window, 1976 to 1988. However, it sat unloved for decades, with many enthusiasts citing its lackluster performance and what they erroneously called its van-derived engine as solid proof that it wasn't a "proper" Porsche.

In a recent development, the eventual 924 Turbo and homologation special 924 Carrera GT models did much to align the little coupé with enthusiasts, but for our purposes here, it's the naturally aspirated 2.0-liter inline-4-powered model that appeals the most. The Classics World 924 Buyer's Guide describes it as remarkably robust, and claims "simple DIY maintenance" is often all that's required to keep it running. The guide adds that 924 spare parts are available directly through the automaker via Porsche's Classic program, and are frequently quite affordable.

Industry observers note that numerous enthusiasts on owners forums are happy to boast that their own pride-and-joys have been able to surpass 100,000 miles, and often by some serious margins. One post on Porsche Club Great Britain details both a 168,000-mile and 272,000-mile example, and that post is almost 20 years old, so many more examples may well have hit such achievements since. Owner reviews further back up the 924's claim to indestructibility, saying that, in spite of its age, the little Porsche largely proves very dependable across long ownership windows.

While the Porsche 924 is impressively reliable and durable, it probably isn't the adrenaline-fueled sports car that springs into most minds when the word "Porsche" is uttered. Instead, something like the original 930 Turbo is far more appropriate.

According to recent reports, it was produced between the 1975 and '89 model years, and throughout that time the engine evolved from a turbocharged 3.0-liter flat-6 with 256 horsepower into a boosted 3.3-liter unit that produced 296 horses. U.S. versions received slightly less power, but these were still very formidable sports cars for the era.

In a recent development, turbochargers do add extra complexity into engines, and they can fail prematurely, so it might be reasonable to assume the 930 Turbo doesn't fall into the "indestructible" category. Well, you'd be wrong to assume that, and one man alone proves that point impeccably. His name is Bill MacEachern, and he ordered a 930 Turbo back when they were new in '76. He's kept it ever since, and racked up in excess of 826,000 miles during that time. Yes, its engine has been rebuilt, but he's had it tuned to produce in excess of 550 horsepower, and it's still managing its daily duties without stress. Here he is on Magnacars telling the story:.

In a recent development, those seeking to find themselves an indestructible 930 Turbo for piling on the miles should head for a 3.3-liter model. These received internal improvements over the earlier cars, like different sealing rings that could deal with heat more effectively, enabling the engine to handle its performance more reliably. Also, the addition of an intercooler massively reduced intake temperatures on 3.3-powered cars, as well as helping to bring that extra grunt.

Sources indicate that if a boosted Porsche 911 from the late '70s is capable of punching out 800,000-plus miles, it stands to reason that a less performance-focused 911 of the same era also makes for a pretty dependable companion. The SC introduced new technologies and developments in the engine bay that really helped boost reliability.

Sources indicate that the previous model was powered by a 2.7-liter mill, the last evolution of the 911's original engine. By this point, it was at its limit, and with thermal reactors used to help reduce emissions in line with new legislation, heat was a major issue. This heat buildup caused head stud and valve issues, and while fixable via the aftermarket route, such issues plagued the reliability reputation of early '70s 911s. The later SC rectified this issue with an all-aluminum engine casing that could better handle the engine's higher temperatures, and those thermal reactors were replaced with catalytic converters, which ran far cooler.

According to recent reports, it's well-documented that these 3.0-liter SC models are good for 200,000 miles or more between engine rebuilds, as long as they are suitably maintained. So if it's an early 911 with built-in indestructibility that you're seeking, this is a far better starting point than any pre-'77 car. In fact, Porsche Club GB describes the 3.0-liter as "probably the most reliable Porsche engine ever" and "simple to work on." Just be prepared for the prices commanded; we recently found a 164,000-mile 911 SC selling for close to $75,000, so even with high mileage, these cars are still a significant investment.

This next entry steers us back away from Porsche's legendary line of rear-engined flat-6-powered models, and once again to a four-cylinder front-engined sports coupé. The Porsche 944, much like the 924, was available in a variety of guises, but for reliability and durability, the simple naturally aspirated models appeal the most.

According to recent reports, its 2.5-liter engine (displacement grew throughout production) is derived from the V8-powered 928, and it's known to have a remarkably strong bottom end. While the Turbo cars aren't exactly fragile, these later boosted engines are more complex, and failures can and do occur, as both turbo exhaust manifolds and wastegates can crack. In terms of what a base 944 can achieve, it's well-documented that these engines are good for in excess of 250,000 miles before a rebuild is necessary, provided necessary maintenance is kept up with along the way.

Recent findings suggest that looking at owner reviews, the 944 experience seems to be mostly trouble-free. Across 127 reviews on CarSurvey, the 944 received a 7.5 out of 10 score for reliability. One owner of a high-mileage example noted that, while certain items like locks, alarms, and other accessories were beginning to fail, they were easily DIY-able, and no power train concerns were noted, despite the car having north of 160,000 miles.

Recent findings suggest that some owners would say a 160,000-mile 944 is still just being broken in. In 2023 a 571,000-mile example was spotted at an auto auction, and even boosted models have been seen with 400,000 miles on the clock, who knows how far a well-maintained 944 can go?

The 3.2-powered Carrera models follow on from the SC, which is a textbook example of an indestructible Porsche. The Carrera 3.2 is less bulletproof than the earlier 3.0 SC, with some experts suggesting it may need top-end work by 130,000 miles, whereas SC cars can exceed that mileage and more without having to come apart. That doesn't mean, however, that the Carrera 3.2 isn't worthy of a place here.

In fact, the 3.2-liter engine received a plethora of updates that 3.0-liter engines miss out on. Fresh pistons, hydraulic timing chain tensioners, and a new Bosch Motronic engine management system were chief among the updates, bringing more power, efficiency, and reliability, especially in the timing system.

In a recent development, regardless of whether the Carrera 3.2 is as bulletproof as its 3.0-liter SC predecessor, it's a fine place to look for a durable classic Porsche. While some do argue the top end may need work by 130,000 miles, others say 200,000 miles is perfectly possible before a rebuild is required. A very smart 218,000-mile example sold this year at auction in the U.K., described by Historics Auctioneers as "One of the best maintained G Series cars we have offered." Admittedly, it had been treated to an engine rebuild and glass-out repaint in recent years, so both its engine and body should be good for another 200,000 miles or so.

The last two entries on our list bring things back up to date, at least a little. While the latest batch of Porsches very well could be the holy grail of reliability and indestructibility, they simply haven't been on the road long enough to prove it, which is why most models here are far older. They've had the chance to accumulate hundreds of thousands of miles and demonstrate their strength.

According to recent reports, one such model is the first-generation Porsche Cayenne, specifically the 3.2-liter model. It's powered by Volkswagen's 30-year-old VR6 engine, which was already well-known by the time Porsche's 955-generation Cayenne debuted as a 2004 model. Why the 3.2? Well, it boasts a strong cast-iron block, whereas the V8 models sported aluminum blocks, and serious engine concerns are quite uncommon.

The 3.2-liter VR6 engine is certainly capable of completing 200,000 miles with basic maintenance covered, and what's just as reassuring, is that the rest of the Cayenne seems built just as tough. One owner on Pistonheads thoroughly detailed every expense during their 51,000-mile and five-year ownership of a Cayenne 3.2 that was already 100,000 miles and 10 years into life when purchased. Apart from general servicing, some tidying up, and a few minor repairs, the Cayenne wanted for nothing, and was sold on to continue its service. Porsche's brand-new Cayenne Turbo Electric might be an impressive $200,000 powerhouse of excellence, but if robust dependability is called for, perhaps its nameplate forefather is the better bet.

We called the 2024 Porsche 718 Boxster GTS 4.0 perfection on wheels, and while it's not a model that's attracting much negative attention to itself, it's barely old enough to call reliable yet, let alone indestructible. The 987.2-generation of Boxster and Cayman, though, is another matter altogether, especially in base 2.9-liter flat-6 guise. While the 3.4-liter "S" model is a better performer, it has been known to suffer bore-scoring, while the 2.9-liter lump seems to avoid that costly concern. Porsche specialist LN Engineering indicates it has "never seen a case of cylinder bore scoring with these models," when referring to the 987.2 Cayman and Boxster.

It's also key to detail why it's the 987.2 cars which deserve a spot here, rather than the 987.1 models. The later models employed an all-new 9A1 engine, which did away with the troublesome IMS bearing altogether. All previous iterations of the Boxster and Cayman were motivated by M96 and M97 engines, which did suffer from IMS problems.

It would appear most owners find the rest of the car to be just as dependable. Across 12 reviews on Cars, specifically for 2010 model-year Boxsters, owners rated the drop-top a respectable 4.4 out of 5 on reliability. Most comments commended the car's sublime road manners, but some did point out their Boxster had been nothing but reliable, which should reassure potential future owners.

#110836. Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (954 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

Europe’s Modelled €5.70/kg Hydrogen Faces Industrial Buyers Who Can Afford Far Less

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (954 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Europe’s industrial hydrogen plans have a buyer problem.
  • The central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg.
  • At a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Europe’s industrial hydrogen plans have a buyer problem. A factory cannot make its products competitive by paying whatever a upcoming hydrogen plant needs to recover its investment. Its maximum hydrogen price is set by the cost of making the same product, or delivering the same useful heat, another way.

The central 2050 scenario in my European hydrogen assessment puts on-site production at €5.70/kg. That starts with electricity at €60/MWh and 53 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen, so the electricity alone costs €3.18/kg. Electrolysers, capital recovery, maintenance, stack replacements, water and other plant costs bring the total to €5.70. Getting hydrogen to a customer can cost more.

At a factory using hydrogen for process heat, €5.70/kg is an expensive fuel. With 94% heating efficiency, delivering one MWh of useful heat requires roughly 31.9 kg of hydrogen. The fuel bill reaches €182/MWh before the burner, maintenance and other equipment costs. In the model’s central 2050 comparison, suitable direct-electric heating sets a hydrogen price ceiling of €2.07/kg. At that ceiling the same hydrogen heat costs about €66/MWh. The hydrogen production case overshoots the customer’s competitive input price by €3.63/kg.

The mismatch is not a prediction that hydrogen makers will never lower costs. It is the actual commercial test investors should apply before financing supply. Reducing the cost of production from €7 to €5 a kilogram achieves little if the relevant industrial customer can pay €2. Production-cost targets are meaningless without a corresponding market price ceiling.

It has been revealed that the International Energy Agency’s Global Hydrogen Review 2026 has made customer cost acceptability part of its assessment. Across most sector and region comparisons, the IEA finds maximum acceptable hydrogen prices below US$2/kg without policy support. Some incumbent-steel comparisons yield negative acceptable prices. The IEA examines a 2035 horizon and a different set of competitors; the same buyer-side arithmetic exposes the problem.

Industry observers note that my TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment calculates the maximum hydrogen input price for industrial heat, ammonia and ironmaking and compares it with distinct European supply cases. It also links to the underlying European hydrogen research and interactive model.

Sources indicate that european ammonia illustrates how demand for a product differs from demand for European-made hydrogen. Ammonia remains necessary for fertilisers and industrial chemicals. The buyer’s real choice is where to produce it. In the central 2050 TFIE model, making qualifying green ammonia inside Europe can compete with imported green ammonia only when its hydrogen input costs roughly €2.62–€4.00/kg, depending on the origin and production route. The €5.70/kg onsite supply case misses those thresholds. Europe can keep consuming ammonia without building every electrolyser locally.

According to recent reports, ironmaking has a similar sourcing decision. The model’s hydrogen input-price ceiling versus qualifying imported hydrogen-reduced or hot-briquetted iron ranges from €2.28 to €4.45/kg. Against a European electrochemical iron process, the central ceiling is approximately €1.43/kg. Where enough suitable scrap can deliver the required steel grade, the hydrogen-based route can lose even at a zero price for hydrogen. Steel quality, industrial integration and the commercial maturity of electrochemical iron matter to those comparisons. They do not entitle a hydrogen supplier to ignore the alternatives.

Industry observers note that hydrogen used as a chemical reagent deserves a different assessment from hydrogen burned for heat. Chemical production may need the molecule. Industrial heating needs temperature, pressure, reliability and useful energy, all of which can be delivered directly from electricity for many applications. Manufacturing hydrogen from electricity and then burning it adds conversion losses and fuel-system costs before the plant receives the heat it needs.

Recent findings suggest that the supply cases have defined boundaries. The central onsite cost is €5.70/kg. A generic delivery allowance takes that case to €6.95/kg. The model’s separately configured hub-and-pipeline case is €5.81/kg. Those are different cost structures, not interchangeable price quotes for the same customer. Even the favourable 2050 case, at €3.46/kg with its specified delivery allowance and €28/MWh electricity, clears some industrial thresholds but still misses others.

It has been revealed that policy can create demand that market prices do not support. Carbon pricing, procurement mandates, subsidies and carbon contracts for difference can raise willingness or obligation to pay. That may be a deliberate industrial or climate choice, but governments should disclose the premium, who will finance it and the contract duration. Describing a regulated purchase as competitive demand hides the cost rather than eliminating it.

Industry observers note that the EU energy regulators’ market monitoring points in the same direction. ACER reported 4.2 GW of committed electrolyser capacity in November 2026, including operating plants, projects under construction and those with final investment decisions. Roughly 49% was associated with refining, where renewable-fuel mandates provide a strong demand signal. The remaining industrial sectors face a harder test when policy does not compel the same purchases.

For lenders, the consequence is immediate. A proposed hydrogen plant costing €5/kg has no viable commercial case when its intended industrial buyer can afford €3/kg. A memorandum of understanding cannot close that €2/kg gap. Developers need buyers with enforceable contracts at prices that cover supply costs, lower production costs, or identified support durable enough to finance the difference.

Industrial and public procurement should start with the product the customer must deliver, calculate the best eligible competing route, and determine the maximum hydrogen price that route permits. Only then should investors consider electrolysers, pipelines and capacity targets. Suppliers do not set the market by drawing cheaper future cost curves. Industrial customers set the ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that the full TFIE Briefing and open European hydrogen assessment contain the industrial route comparisons, scenario assumptions and research submitted to the European Commission. The next Briefing examines the competing routes for sourcing green ammonia and iron.

#110835. Industry News: 7 Luxury Cars Most Likely To Last 200,000 Miles

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2087 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: 7 Luxury Cars Most Likely To Last 200,000 Miles

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Buying a newly introduced car is more expensive than ever, and if you want something from an established luxury or premium brand, it's going to cost you even more.
  • However, just because you spend big bucks on a luxury vehicle doesn't mean it will be reliable.
  • According to recent reports, we examined reliability ratings, longevity studies, and ownership data from various sources, including an iSeeCars study on the longest-lasting models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Buying a newly introduced car is more expensive than ever, and if you want something from an established luxury or premium brand, it's going to cost you even more. Of course, when you're spending more, you expect to get more in return. On top of the prestige that comes with driving a luxury brand, you're probably expecting nicer materials, more equipment, and a better dealership experience when compared to mainstream brands. And another thing you want for your money is a vehicle that lasts. If you are spending big bucks for an Audi or Mercedes-Benz, you should expect it to last for 200,000 miles without needing three transmissions, two engine rebuilds, and a daily prayer.

However, just because you spend big bucks on a luxury vehicle doesn't mean it will be reliable. Just ask anyone who's owned a Land Rover after the original warranty expired. On the other hand, you don't need to resign yourself to driving a Toyota Corolla if you want to see 200,000 miles displayed on your odometer. The trick is knowing which luxury vehicles you should take a chance on, and that's what this list is all about.

According to recent reports, we examined reliability ratings, longevity studies, and ownership data from various sources, including an iSeeCars study on the longest-lasting models. You'll see SUVs, wagons, and sedans on this list, although you'll also only see a few cars from the same manufacturer. Otherwise, this would pretty much just be a list of current Lexus models. Lexus does make some very reliable vehicles, but its cars are not the only options if you want something that lasts.

In a recent development, the Acura MDX has a 13.1% chance of reaching 250,000 miles. Although that's a relatively low percentage, it's 2.4 times better than the average vehicle and 50,000 miles above what this list is looking for. In other words, reaching the 200,000-mile mark is a very achievable feat for this model. The three-row luxury SUV starts at $53,350, which includes the destination and handling fee. It might not get front row parking at the finest restaurant in town, but the MDX can be loaded up with luxury touches if you opt for certain packages. Those touches include open-pore wood accents, contrast stitching on the Milano leather interior, and a premium Bang & Olufsen Sound System, as well as a panoramic moonroof which comes standard on all models.

The front-wheel-drive MDX is powered by a 3.5-liter V6 producing 290 horsepower and 267 pound-feet of torque. That's also the case for its all-wheel-drive A-Spec trim, which can be kitted out with even more niceties like a surround-view camera and 20-inch wheels. The highest-end model you can get is the Type S Advance, which gets a twin-scroll turbocharged 3.0-liter V6 good for 355 horses and 354 pound-feet. A Type S with just about every option tops out around $80,000. None of these features are particularly cutting-edge, but that's exactly why this SUV is so reliable. Another feather in the cap of the MDX is that it's safe, too, with the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) naming it a Top Safety Pick. It isn't the flashiest luxury vehicle out there, but it will do everything it needs to do for as long as you need it to.

According to recent reports, it might be surprising to see an Audi on this list. After all, German cars don't typically hold the same reliability reputation as the Japanese automakers, with Consumer Reports giving new Audi vehicles a middling ranking when it comes to predicted reliability. However, some models from the brand fare better than others. The Audi S3 ranked as the most reliable luxury subcompact car under $60,000, per iSeeCars. To be fair, only two cars were in that category, but it also ranked eighth among 35 luxury small cars for reliability. Most of the cars ranked above it are either out of production or Lexus models that aren't being included on this list to keep it from being too Lexus-centric.

Kelley Blue Book (KBB) rated the 2025 Audi S3 as number one in the Best Luxury Compact Cars category based on performance, reliability, safety and other factors. The manufacturer also gave the Audi S3 an above-average reliability rating, while S3 owners on the website gave it a perfect five out of five score. All in all, it isn't unreasonable to expect this model to reach 200,000 miles.

It has been revealed that powering the $53,895 Audi S3 is the fourth-generation EA888 engine. The turbocharged DOHC 16-valve inline-four makes 328 horsepower and 295 pound-feet of torque. It will rocket to 60 mph in just over four seconds, but it has a lot more going for it than straight-line speed. Inside is a 15-speaker Sonos sound system and the Audi Virtual Cockpit plus. Optionally, you can add Nappa leather seats for $1,000 and a Driver Assistance package that includes surround view cameras and adaptive cruise control for $1,800.

It has been revealed that no automaker is perfect, but it's hard to argue against how dominant Toyota and Lexus are when it comes to reliability. In the aforementioned iSeeCars study on vehicle reliability, nine of the top 10 vehicles are either Toyota or Lexus models. The Lexus GX in particular has a 23.3% chance of reaching 250,000 miles, which is 4.3 times higher than average. The redesigned GX 550 arrived for the 2024 model year with a twin-turbocharged 3.4-liter V6 and substantially more modern technology. You could argue that the upcoming generation GX has not been out long enough to determine true long-term reliability, but the reputation of Lexus has earned this model some leeway to make it onto this list.

According to recent reports, the GX is a traditional body-on-frame SUV that offers genuine off-road ability and the strength to endure many years of trail bashing. All GX trims, including the entry-level $69,085 GX 550 Premium, get the same engine making 349 horsepower and 479 pound-feet of torque. With the over-$76,000 Overtrail trim, the GX can tow up to 9,096 pounds, which is within 150 pounds of a Ford F-150 SuperCrew 4x4 with the 5.0-liter V8 engine. Alternatively, the over-$81,000 Luxury trim will get you heated and ventilated semi-aniline leather seats that have massage functionality, as well as a 21-speaker Mark Levinson sound system.

Sources indicate that the Lexus IS is an interesting car because it has plenty of luxury features to justify the Lexus badge and price point — and yet, it is surprisingly old-school. There are no turbochargers or hybrid systems to add complexity. Under the hood is a naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 from the legendary Toyota 2GR engine series. In other words, getting a couple hundred thousand miles out of this engine should be no sweat. And the iSeeCars study agrees, as the IS has a 17.5% chance to reach 250,000 miles – 3.3 times higher than average.

It has been revealed that starting at $47,545, the IS is the least-expensive Lexus sedan in the current lineup. But that doesn't stop it from including all the luxury touches you would expect from the brand. That includes the standard Forged Bamboo center console, the 12.3-inch touchscreen, and a matching digital instrument cluster. Extra luxuries like the 17-speaker Mark Levinson audio system can be found in the Special Appearance Package, which will run you a little over $60,000. It's a good pick if you're looking for something fancy that will also let you circumnavigate the Earth eight times over.

Sources indicate that historically, if you wanted a luxury car to last at least 200,000 miles, you'd just buy a Lexus LS. It might not be the fanciest car in the world, but it's practically as reliable than the sunrise — and it's probably the most likely car on this list to make it to that mileage target. It has a 38.8% chance of reaching 250,000 miles, putting it 7.2 times higher than the average car. On top of that, iSeeCars measured the Lexus LS 500 as having an average lifespan of 226,558 miles. Yes, even the average LS 500 is likely to break the 200,000-mile barrier. Go back in history and you will find some that go much further, like Matt Farah's LS 400, which managed to cross the million-mile threshold.

Though, the biggest hurdle to getting a Lexus LS 500 to last for 200,000 miles might be actually buying one. The LS lineup is going out of production after nearly 40 years, and to mark the occasion, Lexus is building just 250 Heritage Edition LS 500s. At $99,280, you won't get much change back from your $100,000 bill. But you will get a panoramic glass roof, a Laser Special Black premium wood trim, a 23-speaker Mark Levinson Surround Sound system, and more. Plus, like all LS 500s, you'll get a twin-turbocharged 3.4-liter V6 that makes 416 horsepower and 442 pound-feet of torque. It's a shame to see the LS go, but given its history of reliability, you'll likely still see it on the road for decades to come.

While every Mercedes-Benz may not be a paragon of reliability, there are some models that stand above the rest. We put the Mercedes-Benz E-Class Wagon on this list not just because it is reliable, but also because it's one of the best station wagons of all time. Wagons only make up about 1% of fresh vehicle sales in the U.S., yet the people who buy them tend to love them and want to keep them for a while. For those folks, the Mercedes-Benz E-Class Wagon is an excellent choice.

The E-Class wagon has a 7.5% chance to hit 250,000 miles, which is 2.2 times higher than average. Additionally, the iSeeCars recall study lists the E-Class as one of the least likely vehicles to be recalled over a 30-year lifespan, with an expected recall rate of just 0.2 in those three decades. For the sake of comparison, the Lincoln Aviator has a recall rate of 94.2 recalls during that same time span. Not having a vehicle recalled doesn't mean it will last for 200,000 miles, but it does reflect the model's attention to detail and build quality.

For the E-Class's most luxurious offerings, a latest 2027 E 450 4MATIC All-Terrain starts at $81,450. It comes with standard features such as dual-zone climate control, a panorama roof, and a power liftgate. You can also add ventilated and massaging front seats, Nappa leather upholstery, and more features if your budget can handle it (with an increase of $2,600 for the top-of-the-line Pinnacle trim). It's all powered by an engine making 375 horsepower and 369 pound-feet of torque. If you have an extra $15,000 to spare, there's also a hybrid model available with even more luxury features, and its horsepower and torque figures increase to 577 and 553, respectively.

Industry observers note that today, you can get an SUV from just about every automaker, from Aston Martin to Rolls-Royce. But the Mercedes-Benz G-Class is still one of the most luxurious off-road SUVs you can buy, and unlike some others, it can also handle some very challenging terrain. The G-Class has a 17.3% estimated chance of reaching 250,000 miles, which is more than three times the average. The Mercedes-Benz G-Class also has an average lifespan of 187,916 miles, so 200,000 is not much of a stretch. iSeeCars ranked it number one out of 18 vehicles in the Most Reliable Luxury Large SUVs category. Plus, the G-Class has the same minuscule expected recall rate as the E-Class.

Industry observers note that none of this comes cheap, though. The least expensive G-Class, with 443 horsepower and 413 pound-feet of torque, starts at over $153,000. Sure, buying a significant, heavy vehicle like this can save you thousands on your taxes. And that substantial starting price includes luxuries such as leather upholstery, heated front seats and armrests, three-zone climate control, and heated and cooled cup holders. But the G-Class will also be on the expensive side to operate. You need to fill it with premium gas, and fuel economy runs in the teens. You'll also be paying Mercedes-Benz prices for maintenance and service.

Still, if you stay on top of it, the G-Class should last a very long time — and that goes for any vehicle on this list. If you want them to last 200,000 or even 300,000 miles, following the maintenance schedule is just one tip that you should follow. Doing that will help these already reliable vehicles last for even longer.

#110833. EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October

EV & Auto 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cleantechnica ↗ Open Full Page

EV Share Jumps to 68%(!) and Small BEVs Rise to Power — China EV Sales Report for October

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!
  • This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash.
  • Adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

High gas prices and a never-ending wave of new BEVs have allowed October to reach 68% EV market share, a new record!

This record achievement is thanks to a significant ICE (internal combustion engine) crash. The overall market dropped 27% year over year (YoY), to around 1.6 million sales. Plugins were down 14% YoY, but pure ICE sales were much worse off, crashing 44% YoY!

Adding 45% BEV share to PHEVs (23% share) meant that in October a record 68% of all cars sold in China had a plug! If this trend continues in the future, the Chinese market will be fully electrified by 2030, and will be 100% BEV before 2035!

This great result pulled the 2026 share up, to 59%, already 5% above the full year result of 2025. BEVs on their own were up to 40% (versus 33% in 2025).

At this pace, I expect the final number for 2026 EV share in China to be above 60%, with BEVs alone north of the 40% mark. And when the largest global automotive market gets this electrified … then the ICE industry is in serious trouble.

The ICE extinction is also visible in the overall ranking. The overall top 10 was fully made by EVs. Again.

According to recent reports, looking at the best sellers in several size categories, the ICE extinction is also quite visible. Although, once again, the C-segment/compact category is the exception, with the only ICE representative showing up there — the Toyota RAV4, in 2nd, behind the leader Nevo Q05 and just ahead of the BYD Dolphin.

Having a quick look at the five size categories, the highlight is the B-segment/subcompact category, which is the hottest segment right now, with three of the top four top sellers in October belonging to this category.

Considering that 56% of the fresh SUVs launched this year were bigger than 5 meters/197 inches, there is a clear disconnect between what people want (small hatchbacks/crossovers) and what OEMs offer (large SUVs).

Another highlight is the fact that Xiaomi had a gold plus silver win in the full size category, with the BYD Great Tang closing out the podium while the midsize category podium was 100% BYD Group.

Here’s more info and commentary on October’s top selling electric models:.

A BYD Dolphin for BYD Seagull money ($10,000). This was Geely’s internal memo to describe the formula for the Geely Xingyuan when developing its star model. With an interesting name — Xingyuan translates as “wishing upon a star” — it seems that Geely had its wish granted. However, the Geely model will have a tough adversary soon, as the fresh generation Seagull will land with only one goal — to steal the Xingyuan’s best seller status. But while the new Seagull didn’t land, the small Geely scored a record performance in October, with its 50,190 registrations representing a 14% increase YoY. Besides the new BYD Seagull, Geely’s hatchback now has to deal with Leapmotor’s B-segment contenders, the A10 and A05; the new-generation Wuling Bingo; Chery’s new QQ3; and let’s not forget about BYD’s Yuan Up, too.

Sources indicate that BYD’s midsize SUV continues to transition into the newly introduced generation. Thanks to the ramp-up of the new Ultra body, BYD’s star player was 2nd, scoring 30,772 registrations. Sales were up by 6% compared to the same month last year. The new Ultra generation features lidar and 1,500 kW DC charging, and these two features aren’t even the most impressive aspects of the model! That would be the price. It starts at 152,000 yuan (or $22,000) with the 76 kWh battery, and it goes up to 180,000 yuan (or $26,000) with the 83 kWh battery. For comparison, the Tesla Model Y starts in China at 259,000 yuan ($38,250)…. Expect the Song to experience a second youth from here onwards, and while it is impossible to displace the Tesla Model Y from the runner-up spot, the last place on the podium is doable this year. And maybe higher up in 2027?

In a recent development, BYD’s small crossover continues to surprise, thanks to recently improved specs. BYD’s team player rose to 3rd in October, scoring 28,514 registrations, which was a 44% increase YoY and a newly introduced record score. Despite not being the most exciting vehicle to look at, or drive, the truth is that it is surfing the wave of small, affordable EVs better than most, scoring high in value for money with prices starting at $11,000 and higher end versions having BYD’s driver-assistance system. With small vehicles right now having a moment in China, expect the small crossover to show up in the top 5 more regularly.

Industry observers note that things continue to go well for the startup brand, with its new baby A10 now established as the star player in an already strong lineup. Thanks to 27,247 registrations, the small crossover managed another top 5 presence. The model has the usual value-for-money focus of the brand, and a low, low price of 66,000 yuan ($10,000). On top of that, however, the A10 offers something close to a distinct personality, as the design eschews the white product standard design of Leapmotor for something more personal, mostly thanks to the front and back lights and a floating roof effect. With B-segment BEVs now being the hottest category in China, Leapmotor is well prepared to benefit from the subcompact rising tide, thanks to the recent arrival of the A10 small crossover and its sibling, the A05 small hatchback. Talk about perfect timing….

In a recent development, after the SU7 and YU7, Xiaomi has another success on its hands. This big fat SUV — or shall I say SUVs, as the lineup is broken down between the 7-seat N90 and the 5-seat N70 — scored 27,132 registrations in only its second month on the market, pulling it immediately into the overall top 5. Even with the number of competitors growing every passing day, Xiaomi’s new land yachts have been selling like hot cakes, while drying up sales of the competition. Proof of that, is the fact that there were only two full size models in October’s top 20, with the other being … the Xiaomi SU7.

Looking at the rest of the best seller table, there were a number of models hitting record scores, starting with the #8 Nevo Q05 (20,022 units) continuing its success story. The #10 Bestune Xiaoma (17,887 units) benefitted from a recent refresh to score a surprise record score. Could this mean that small city EVs are (finally) seeing the light at the end of the tunnel?

As for the second half of the table, the highlight is the ramp-up of the Xpeng L03, with the attractive looking crossover, which kind of reminds of a mini-Lotus or small Polestar, reaching 13th thanks to 15,653 sales. This EV looks to be the startup’s star model thanks to a competitive price (124,000 RMB) that is half the price of the Tesla Model Y!

Other models with record performances were the #14 MG 4 (15,503 units), with the newly introduced generation proving to be much more popular and adaptable to local tastes than the previous one, and the #17 Chery QQ3 EV, which continued its slow climb in the ranking thanks to 14,041 sales, which made it the 5th B-segment model in the top 20.

According to recent reports, still in the top 20, we should also highlight the best selling foreign model, the Tesla Model Y VW ID.Aura T6, the new China-made (and China-developed) German crossover that has allowed Volkswagen to beat the Texans for the first time in years (the Tesla Model Y was down 60% YoY, to 7,807 units, while the Model 3 was down 85%, to 1,010 units). The Aura T6, VW’s take on the Model Y formula, rose to the 20th position in its first full month on the market!

A promising sign, or just hype? Only time will tell, but at least for now, VW seems to be getting some traction on the EV side of the Chinese market, a point also highlighted by the fact that it wasn’t just the Aura T6 getting decent sales. The also upcoming VW ID.Era 5S (think Chinese VW Jetta) got 7,100 registrations in October. Is there hope after all?

Outside the top 20, the main event was the ramp-up of Nevo’s newly introduced baby, the Q06, which is looking to replicate the Q05’s success in the category above. With some 10,000 registrations in only its second month, it looks like it could join the top 20 soon. The same can be said about the Geely Galaxy TT, the make’s answer to the Xiaomi SU7, which had around 10,500 deliveries in October. Then there’s also the BYD Yuan Plus, which, after a long cross through the desert, seems to be picking up steam again. It scored 11,658 registrations last month, a new year best.

Sources indicate that looking at the 2026 ranking, the podium remained the same, and unless something unexpected happens, it should stay as it is until the end of the year, with the small Geely repeating its 2025 win. That also means the Tesla Model Y will return to silver after getting bronze in 2025, and the BYD Song will get back onto the podium after a one-year absence.

Below the podium positions, though, there was some news. The BYD Yuan Up and Leapmotor A10 are surfing the B-segment wave and both climbed a position, to 5th and 6th, respectively.

If the BYD Yuan Up continues on its current record streak, then the small crossover could even aim to surpass the #4 FCB Ti7 before the year ends.

Still, with three subcompacts right now in the top 6 (Geely Xingyuan, BYD Yuan Up, and Leapmotor A10), small is hot right now, in China.

Elsewhere, the BYD Sealion 05 was up two positions, to 16th, while the Wuling Mini EV is hoping to bring tiny city cars back into the spotlight, and in October, it jumped two positions, ending the month in 13th….

Looking at the overall manufacturer ranking, it is a sea of red. Everyone is losing sales — massive time. The exception is #5 Leapmotor (+31% YoY), while #8 Xiaomi (+3% YoY) and #10 Xpeng (+0%) are just hanging on.

So, now, not only are foreign OEMs suffering (Nissan was down 70% in October, Honda was down 51%), but even domestic ones are being affected by the EV shift.

Some may be asking, “But what about #9 Nevo and its 125% growth rate?” Well, it isn’t so much that they are winning sales, but they are effectively replacing the sales of their mother brand, Changan, which in October was only 19th after a 60% drop in sales YoY.

Looking at the auto brand ranking, BYD is firmly in the leadership position (17.2%), while runner-up Geely held to its 7.1% market share.

In a recent development, rising 3rd placed Leapmotor (6.7%, up 0.2%) is fast approaching Geely. It wouldn’t be surprising if the startup brand became the fresh silver medalist in the final days of the year.

Industry observers note that one thing is for certain though — Leapmotor will win its first medal this year. The only question is the material that it will be made of….

Speaking of position changes, Tesla had a horrible month (4.4%, down from 4.9% in September), which allowed Wuling (4.6%) to climb one position in October, into 4th. At the end of the year, expect Tesla to keep the #4 position, as its December peak should help it surpass Wuling.

Looking at OEMs/automotive groups/alliances, BYD is leading with 21.9% share of the market, up 0.1% in October.

Meanwhile, Geely remained in second with 11.8% share. The multinational conglomerate has the runner-up spot secured.

Industry observers note that #3 SAIC was stable (8%) and remained firm in the last place on the podium, while #4 Leapmotor (6.7%, up 0.2%) remained on the rise. Will we see the startup challenge SAIC in 2027 for the 3rd spot?

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

For any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

Nobody Knows What This Space Object Is Or Why It Can Move Against Gravity

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A small object orbiting the Sun has long befuddled scientists, and recent research has simply befuddled them more.
  • Whatever it is, it's about 36 feet across.
  • Industry observers note that oh, and there's the minor detail that it's accelerating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A small object orbiting the Sun has long befuddled scientists, and recent research has simply befuddled them more. Called 1998 KY26 and discovered that year by astronomer Tom Gehrels of the University of Arizona, it is quite simply not following the laws of gravitational dynamics. In other words, it's accelerating, someway, somehow. Multiple theories have been proposed as to what could be happening, but with latest evidence coming in, none of those theories quite seem to fit. It's probably not aliens. But it just might be communists.

So, what do we know for sure? Not much. Whatever it is, it's about 36 feet across. That bit is relatively fresh information, since scientists initially estimated it was about three times larger, per the BBC's Sky at Night Magazine. It's also in a very rapid spin, rotating about once every five minutes. It has a very high albedo (no jokes, straight to jail with you), meaning that it reflects more sunlight than is typical for a space object. Earth's Moon, which lights up your night, reflects 12% of the sunlight it receives; 1998 KY26 reflects about 50%.

Industry observers note that oh, and there's the minor detail that it's accelerating. Again, there are theories about what it is, but none of them fit quite right.

Sources indicate that comets are true cosmic beauties, with their long tails streaking behind them. But those tails aren't just for looking pretty: they are the emissions of the comet's ice, going straight from solid to gas and skipping the liquid water stage altogether ("sublimating"). That process also knocks off particles from the comet's rock, and as the law of conservation of momentum stipulates, shooting these particles away from the comet means the comet experiences a slight push forward. Acceleration! There's just one problem: 1998 KY26 has no tail. Oops.

Fourteen such objects have been discovered in our solar system. Called "dark comets," the thinking is that they are in fact sublimating like a normal comet, but for some reason, the process isn't visible. So, Theory Number 1 is simply that 1998 KY26 is indeed outgassing, you just can't see it (again, no jokes, straight to jail with you).

Case closed? Not quite. Per the Latest York Times, recent research demonstrates that the object has a temperature of minus 53 degrees Fahrenheit, which is far too warm for ice (things are weird in space). If there's no ice, then there's no sublimation, and in fact the object cannot be a comet at all, let alone a dark one. There are other options. But they get weirder.

Here's something you may not have known: photons of light, which have no mass, have momentum. That means that sunlight actually exerts pressure, which might have an appreciable impact on an object's velocity over time. There's also the Yarkovsky effect, or the force generated by emitting heat (in this case, again from sunlight). So Theory Number 2 is that these forces have created enough thrust on 1998 KY26 that it's pushed past where gravity alone would have taken it. The Upcoming York Times quotes NASA as preferring this explanation. Unfortunately, other scientists claim that these effects simply do not provide enough forces to explain the object's acceleration.

Theory Number 3 has the object as an asteroid, not a comet. Remember, this thing is rotating once every five minutes; that's fast enough that it might well be yeeting pieces of itself off into the universe. If, for some reason, that yeeting is all in a similar direction, you'd have extra thrust. But why would the asteroid throw a temper tantrum only in one direction?

It has been revealed that if you have at last reached the "aliens, bro" stage of your thinking, calm down, because not even Harvard's resident alien guy thinks it's them. But he does think it's the Soviets.

Last year, our solar system was visited by an object from the outermost reaches of our galaxy. Called 3I/ATLAS, it drew all manner of speculation as to its nature, but there was one man who questioned its intentions. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb became something of an internet darling for proposing that it was an alien spacecraft. Would you believe he's also got opinions on 1998 KY26? Per Newsweek, he once again does not believe that it's a natural object. But this time he thinks he knows exactly what it is: Phobos 1, a probe intended to study Mars and its moon Phobos for the glory of the Soviet Union in 1988. The glory of Phobos 1 was short-lived, as the proud comrade manning the control console for the probe entered a typo, which deactivated crucial systems and lost them the craft. Spelling matters, kids.

Recent findings suggest that it didn't blow up, but nobody knows where it went. So, with 1998 KY26, we have an object that is roughly the same size, on roughly the right trajectory, that is freakishly reflective. That sure does sound like a metallic probe with solar panels. Theory Number 4 holds that Phobos 1 came to its current orbit via two thruster burns (presumably via faulty circuitry), on September 2, 1988, and May 19, 1996. This is pure conjecture, however, and not that much more sophisticated than "aliens, bro." There is no direct evidence that 1998 KY26 is non-natural. NASA rejects this theory.

Where does that leave us? As with the astrophysicists studying it, it leaves us with more questions than answers. The good news is, Japanese space agency JAXA launched the Hayabusa2 probe to go there and find out what it is once and for all! The bad news is, it's already aborted from that mission due to an engine problem. So the mystery remains, as it slowly orbits the Sun, too quickly for gravity's math, dancing on its own.

Put To The Test, Those Special Engine Cleaning Oils Do Some Lifting

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that motor oil naturally helps to flush out common contaminants, and there's a whole supply of products specifically made to keep the mechanical parts of a vehicle clean and running.
  • The Motor Oil Geek is Lake Speed Jr., of SPEEDiagnostix, known for its used oil analysis services.
  • Using those skills, he put three "cleaning" motor oils up to the test: Mobil 1 Advanced Clean, Valvoline Restore & Protect, and Pennzoil Ultra Platinum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that motor oil naturally helps to flush out common contaminants, and there's a whole supply of products specifically made to keep the mechanical parts of a vehicle clean and running. From Top Tier gasoline complete with detergents to some types of engine motor oil — these treatments and additives are designed and marketed to you, the consumer, to keep things clean internally so your car lasts. Do they really do what they claim to do, though? The Motor Oil Geek on YouTube put those "cleaning" oils to the test to see if they do make a difference.

The Motor Oil Geek is Lake Speed Jr., of SPEEDiagnostix, known for its used oil analysis services. Speed himself is a Certified Lubrication Specialist and OIl Analyst who used that expertise to help Joe Gibbs Racing for 12 years — a testing ground sometimes more brutal than the testing cars go through in-house.

Using those skills, he put three "cleaning" motor oils up to the test: Mobil 1 Advanced Clean, Valvoline Restore & Protect, and Pennzoil Ultra Platinum. There's actually a fourth oil, Valvoline Premium Blue Restore Gen2 — but that's a separate, yet important test, also included in the video. The results didn't match what real in-engine testing produced, but even in this comparable bench testing scenario, these oils managed to clean up expectations.

In a recent development, the Motor Oil Geek put the three oils through what's called an ASTM sequence IIIH test, which is a standard test used to evaluate engine oils at high temperatures and high speeds. Typically, these tests are conducted in an actual running engine for 90 total hours, broken down into four 20-hour test segments and one 10-hour segment. For bench test purposes, Speed ran the oils for 168 hours with varying temperatures from room temperature to 150 degrees Celsius, to better emulate real-time conditions of an engine from cold runs to high-speed performance.

He used pistons with considerable deposits from a turbocharged Mini Cooper engine, each marked with a letter code to track which one was tested in what oil. Those pistons were sent off to be professionally rated before the test, as well as after, to measure improved "cleanliness.".

Three of those pistons were then hung separately from a device so they could soak in an oil in 1000 mL beakers over a magnetic stirring hot plate. It's a way to control the important aspects of the test concerning time, temperature, and agitation (movement), so Speed could focus on the concentration and cleaning. The fourth piston was soaked in the Valvoline Premium Blue Restore Gen2, which claimed it could clean parts just soaked in the oil.

Industry observers note that in the end, all four oils cleaned some of the deposits on the pistons. The most improved was the fourth piston that soaked in the oil, which The Motor Oil Geek explained contains an agent called Ester, also used in two-stroke oils to keep things clean. And keep in mind, they perform even better in a running engine. So, if you're at all worried about buildup slowing you down, these cleaning oils might actually do the trick.

  • According to recent reports, “The first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells are rolling off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan and headed to Louisville Assembly Plant to power Ford Fathom prototypes.
  • Recent findings suggest that “The shipment caps years of work by the team that designed, built, and launched the plant on schedule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ford is now a battery producer. Yes, it’s using battery technology licensed from CATL, but it is now producing EV batteries it is going to be using in its own vehicles. In fact, it is reportedly doing so in a really fast, advanced way. “The BlueOval Battery Park Michigan assembly lines can deliver 40 cells every minute, making it among the fastest LFP prismatic battery assembly lines outside of China.2 That pace helps drive down battery costs, and the facility has capacity for more. But speed must go hand in hand with quality,” Charles Poon, vice president of hardware engineering at Ford, writes.

According to recent reports, “The first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells are rolling off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan and headed to Louisville Assembly Plant to power Ford Fathom prototypes. With this milestone, Ford is now in the battery business and will be the first to deliver LFP batteries in the U.S. for mainstream consumer automotive use,” Poon writes. He goes on to explain further in a recent article why Ford chose to produce LFP battery cells and a bit on how it is doing so. Here’s a bit more from that article:.

Recent findings suggest that “The shipment caps years of work by the team that designed, built, and launched the plant on schedule. Ford now delivers cells at a plant it owns and operates, building expertise to support more affordable electric vehicles (EVs) and Ford Energy’s battery energy storage business in Kentucky.

“Why Start with LFP Prismatic for Fathom?

According to recent reports, “When Alan Clarke, vice president, Advanced Development Projects, first joined the development team that created the Universal Electric Vehicle Platform, he issued a clear challenge: find an efficient LFP prismatic battery. The goal was to make EVs significantly more affordable.

“We talked to battery companies around the world. We wanted a technology that was proven in the field, ready to manufacture at scale, and suited to what we were building. That led us to the world’s leading battery manufacturer, CATL, whose batteries power 30 million vehicles across the globe.

“A battery is one of the biggest contributors to an EV’s cost and weight. So, we asked: How do we get more out of the battery without simply adding more cells? Our answer was efficiency over excess.

“LFP chemistry uses no nickel or cobalt, which helps hold down costs. It also holds up over years of charging and use. That durability is valuable as we give customers ways to use their battery beyond driving. For example, AC bidirectional power lets a vehicle receive electricity from a properly equipped home and supply power back to it.1.

Recent findings suggest that “This milestone is about more than shipping our first cells. We’re building the expertise to produce high-quality batteries at scale — for more affordable EVs and a upcoming energy storage business.”.

It looks like a serious effort and serious progress toward making more affordable, more competitive electric cars at Ford. The aim has been to get as good as making electric cars as Chinese companies are. How effective and successful will this upcoming path be for Ford? We’ll see.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Chris Simms has picked up a $4.5 million Latest York City residence—after offloading his longtime Connecticut estate for $5.5 million.

The 45-year-old—who retired from the NFL in 2010 following a spleen injury—and his wife, Daniella, recently picked up the property, which is located in Sutton Tower.

His newly introduced pad comes complete with three bedrooms, 3.5 bathrooms, and floor-to-ceiling windows, according to the New York Post, who first reported the sale. The property also boasts a chef's kitchen and panoramic views.

The Sutton Place tower was built in 2022 by architect Thomas Juul-Hansen. The residence is known to be the tallest tower on the East Side.

As a member of the luxe dwelling, Simms and his wife get access to a resort-style pool, a gym, a personal training studio, saunas, and a spa space.

His purchase came weeks after Realtor.com® exclusively revealed that he sold his Connecticut property for $5.5 million.

He initially put their longtime Greenwich abode on the market on Feb. 6. Within a matter of months, they had dropped the price by $500,000.

In a recent development, A second price cut in June slashed a further $600,000 from the ask, while a third discount on Aug. 21 saw the athlete's original ask of $8 million lowered to $6.2 million, a move that ultimately bagged a buyer for Simms' dwelling.

Simms, who now serves as an analyst for NBC Sports, purchased the home for $2.5 million in 2019—shortly after he and his wife invested heavily in its restoration and renovation.

The property, which was originally built in 1725, has been updated extensively in the seven years since the couple took ownership.

Today, the property is hailed as a "piece of Greenwich history" with all the luxury of a modern mansion.

"A fully restored antique farmhouse offering approximately 3,669 square feet of refined living space, set on extraordinary level acreage with sweeping meadow views and an irreplaceable country setting across from protected conservation land with direct access to the Greenwich Riding Trails," the listing, which was held by Monica Webster of Douglas Elliman, noted.

The five-bedroom, five-bathroom dwelling features an open floor blueprint that begins with a living area with a cozy fireplace, windows, and wooden beams on the ceiling.

The chef's kitchen boasts state-of-the-art appliances, a white marble island, and white cabinetry.

The charming dining area also has wooden beams on the ceiling and a wooden island.

The bedrooms follow the home's minimalistic aesthetic and feature enough space for a queen-sized bed while boasting small windows.

"The residence blends historic authenticity with modern luxury, featuring wide-plank antique floors, exposed beams, preserved fireplaces, and original architectural details," the listing added.

The bathrooms feature double vanities, a large glass-enclosed shower, a marble soaking tub, and sliding barn doors.

Elsewhere, there is a gym, spa center with a massage chair, and an outdoor entertaining area with a foosball table.

Throughout the home, modern aesthetics have been meticulously merged with historic charm.

"A thoughtful renovation delivers elevated comfort throughout, including a newly created primary suite with cathedral ceilings, floor-to-ceiling windows, a bespoke dressing room, and a private staircase to a serene, light-filled office and library retreat for everyday living," the listing stated.

Simms and his wife lived in Greenwich for many years, having previously sold another dwelling in the area for $2.7 million before relocating to their farmhouse.

They chose the farmhouse for its impressive parcel, noting to the outlet that they wanted more space for their horses.

However, they are now choosing to call to Upcoming York home.

Before settling down in Connecticut, Simms enjoyed a lengthy career in the NFL, a career that began at the University of Texas at Austin, after which he was drafted by the Buccaneers as the last pick of the final round in the 2003 NFL draft.

In a recent development, simms remained with Tampa Bay until 2008, when he was released by the team. He was later picked up by the Tennessee Titans, with whom he played for a year before moving on to the Denver Broncos.

After a brief return to the Titans, the quarterback's career came to an end, with many pointing to a 2006 spleen injury as the reason for his retirement from the NFL.

He briefly tried his hand at coaching, signing with the Fresh England Patriots in 2012 as an offensive coach, as well as a scouting expert, but he made a move into broadcasting after just a few months.

Simms and his wife, who met in high school, tied the knot in 2004 and now share two children.

#110819. Latest Update: Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Enterprise AI is pushing cloud infrastructure beyond the GPU

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1989 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating latest requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure.
  • Agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure.
  • That shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:07 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence is creating latest requirements for enterprise AI infrastructure. While much of the early AI investment centered on access to powerful GPUs, organizations moving AI applications and agents into production are discovering that accelerators are only one part of the equation.

Agentic AI systems need environments where they can execute code, access data, connect to enterprise applications and operate securely across distributed infrastructure. That requires more than bare-metal GPU capacity. It calls for a complete cloud platform that combines compute, networking, storage, security and the services needed to manage applications at scale.

That shift is creating an opportunity for neocloud providers, but it is also changing what enterprises expect from them. Infrastructure providers increasingly need to support the full application lifecycle rather than simply supply specialized hardware.

During a live interview at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026, theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty spoke with Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer at Vultr, about the changing requirements of enterprise AI infrastructure, the return of CPU-based computing, data sovereignty and the growing role of platform engineering.

Industry observers note that “They need a full cloud platform,” Cochrane mentioned. “They need cloud compute, specialized AI compute, networking, storage and an open ecosystem.”.

Vultr entered the cloud market in 2014 with a developer-focused platform built around performance, cost efficiency and accessibility. Since then, the manufacturer has expanded into AI infrastructure, offering both traditional cloud services and specialized GPU resources.

Cochrane remarked Vultr took a deliberate approach to the AI infrastructure market, prioritizing enterprise workload and platform-engineering requirements rather than focusing exclusively on GPU availability.

“We’ve always noted that we’re the tortoise in AI infrastructure,” he said.

According to recent reports, that approach reflects a broader change in how enterprises are approaching AI. Early infrastructure demand largely came from hyperscalers, AI research organizations and startups building large-scale models. Those customers needed access to GPU clusters, often through bare-metal infrastructure.

It has been revealed that the next phase is different. Enterprises are looking to use AI agents to streamline operations, improve customer experiences and create newly introduced revenue opportunities. Those applications must work alongside existing enterprise systems, comply with security requirements and integrate with established network and application architectures.

Recent findings suggest that bare-metal GPU infrastructure alone does not address those needs. Cochrane identified complexity and a lack of specialized skills as major obstacles to enterprise AI adoption. Organizations may have access to powerful accelerators, but they still need the surrounding infrastructure and services to build, deploy and operate applications.

Vultr’s strategy is to provide a more integrated environment, including traditional cloud compute, GPU infrastructure, networking, storage and access to cloud-native projects. Cochrane said the platform supports more than 60 Cloud Native Computing Foundation projects that customers can deploy directly.

The goal is to reduce the work required to assemble an AI environment. Rather than making enterprises integrate every component themselves, providers can offer preconfigured services and composable infrastructure that developers can deploy as needed.

That distinction is becoming vital as AI moves beyond experimentation. Enterprises need infrastructure that supports production applications, not just model training and inference.

Industry observers note that the growing focus on GPUs has sometimes obscured the role of traditional computing resources in AI architectures. But agentic AI is expanding the range of workloads that infrastructure providers must support.

An AI agent does more than send a prompt to a model and receive a response. It may execute scripts, interact with repositories, run builds, access databases and invoke external tools. Those activities require compute resources beyond the GPU.

“Not all workloads need to be on a GPU,” Cochrane noted.

In a recent development, CPUs remain essential for databases, application code and data pipelines. They can also support smaller, optimized open-source models and inference workloads that do not require dedicated accelerators.

According to recent reports, another emerging requirement is the environment in which agents execute tasks. As agents gain the ability to run code and interact with systems, enterprises need secure sandboxes that isolate those activities from production environments and sensitive resources.

Cochrane pointed to work underway in the cloud-native ecosystem around safe and secure agent sandboxes as an indication of how infrastructure requirements are changing.

This creates a more complex infrastructure model. GPUs may handle demanding model reasoning and inference, while CPUs support the applications, pipelines and execution environments surrounding those models.

Industry observers note that for organizations, the implication is that enterprise AI infrastructure decisions should account for the entire agentic workflow. Buying GPU capacity without considering the compute, storage, networking and isolation requirements around it can create another infrastructure silo. A full-stack approach gives platform teams more flexibility to match resources to individual workloads while maintaining a consistent operational environment.

As enterprises expand AI deployments across regions, data sovereignty is becoming more than a question of where information is stored.

Organizations operating in regulated industries or under national data requirements need to understand where data resides, which services can access it and what happens if infrastructure outside a particular region becomes unavailable.

It has been revealed that cochrane described Vultr’s regional architecture as an isolation model in which each of its 34 global data center regions operates independently. According to him, data within a region remains resident there and is not accessed by Vultr services outside that region.

The distinction extends beyond data residency to application operations. Cochrane used France as an example. An application running in a French region should continue operating even if Vultr’s global control plane and its other regions become unavailable.

“If the rest of the world went dark, your production application in France? It just runs,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that that approach is intended to reduce dependencies on global services that could otherwise affect regional application availability. It also gives organizations a clearer boundary for managing sensitive workloads and maintaining operational continuity.

For enterprises, this is an notable architectural consideration. A cloud provider may offer regional data storage, but that does not necessarily mean every service required to operate an application is isolated within the same geography.

As AI applications become more deeply integrated into business operations, organizations will need to evaluate sovereignty across the full application stack, including data, compute, management services and operational dependencies.

The cost of running AI applications is becoming another major consideration as organizations move from pilots to sustained production workloads.

Inference costs can increase swiftly when agents repeatedly call models, retrieve information and execute multi-step workflows. As usage grows, enterprises must balance model performance, throughput and infrastructure expense.

Cochrane believes some organizations will increasingly turn to open-source models that can be adapted to their own data and operated on infrastructure they control. Rather than relying entirely on large commercial models for every task, enterprises can post-train specialized models using proprietary information and deploy them for operational workloads where that approach makes sense.

Sources indicate that he described an example involving a platform engineering organization that reduced inference costs by 80% by post-training an open-source model and running it on its own infrastructure. The example illustrates a potential economic advantage, although results will depend on the workload, model, infrastructure and operational requirements involved.

Recent findings suggest that the broader point is that organizations are beginning to evaluate the economics of enterprise AI infrastructure across the entire stack. Model selection matters, but so do infrastructure utilization, throughput, data movement and the cost of operating agents over time.

For some workloads, owning more of the infrastructure and model lifecycle may provide better cost control than depending entirely on external inference services.

That does not mean every enterprise should build and operate its own models. It does suggest that organizations need more flexibility to choose where models run and how workloads are distributed.

The changing infrastructure requirements of agentic AI are also expanding the responsibilities of platform engineering teams.

Cochrane expects platform engineers to become central to enterprise AI adoption, working more closely with business units to understand which agents and preconfigured application environments are needed across the organization.

Sources indicate that that moves platform engineering beyond infrastructure provisioning and developer enablement. Teams will increasingly need to help define the building blocks that allow developers to deploy governed AI applications without having to assemble every component independently.

It has been revealed that cochrane also sees an opportunity for the cloud-native community to evolve how it shares infrastructure patterns. The CNCF ecosystem has helped developers adopt individual open-source projects across networking, storage, observability and other infrastructure categories. But as architectures become more complex, organizations need guidance on how those components fit together.

Cochrane predicted the emergence of marketplaces where developers can share opinionated, prebuilt stacks for specific workload types. Instead of selecting and configuring individual components, teams could start with a tested architecture and adapt it to their requirements. That could help reduce the complexity of building agentic applications while encouraging more consistent deployment practices.

In a recent development, he also expects consolidation in the neocloud market. Providers focused primarily on bare-metal GPU capacity may face pressure as enterprises demand broader cloud capabilities. Those able to expand into full public cloud platforms could be better positioned to serve production workloads.

Vultr’s existing cloud platform gives it a foundation for that transition, Cochrane said, with its investments in both traditional compute and specialized AI infrastructure.

Enterprise AI is changing the definition of cloud infrastructure. GPUs remain key, but agentic applications require a broader foundation that includes CPUs, secure execution environments, networking, storage, data sovereignty and integrated cloud-native services.

That creates an opportunity for providers that can deliver more than specialized accelerator capacity. It also puts platform engineering teams in a more strategic position as enterprises work to standardize how AI applications are built, deployed and governed.

The next phase of the neocloud market may therefore be determined less by who can offer the most GPU capacity and more by who can provide the complete environment enterprises need to run AI in production.

As Cochrane’s comments suggest, the infrastructure challenge is no longer simply making AI compute available. It is making the entire system around AI practical to operate at enterprise scale.

Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
