💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.
  • In a recent development, scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord.
  • The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook notable problems elsewhere in the body.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

In a recent development, scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook notable problems elsewhere in the body.

It has been revealed that the research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology tech giant Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo notes. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms.".

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss.

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an key question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman notes. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body.".

Recent findings suggest that the peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery.

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a organization co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce key interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

In a recent development, the model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

In a recent development, the scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results highlighted that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance.

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

Sources indicate that these measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

It has been revealed that "You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman states. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection.".

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

In a recent development, however, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important fresh direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research.

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he notes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a seasoned driver, you may be aware that some states' roads are more dangerous in winter.
  • Recent findings suggest that the reason behind the laws is rather simple: Those puffs of smoke in the chilly air indicate a running, usually unlocked, vehicle.
  • It has been revealed that all is not lost for the dedicated puffer, though, as there is an exception to the rule.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a seasoned driver, you may be aware that some states' roads are more dangerous in winter. Did you also know that four out of five of these states, as well as 27 others, have laws against puffing? No, not that puffing. Puffing, or "car puffing," is a slang term for the ritual of letting your car get warm and toasty before driving off. This is usually accomplished by starting your car and then heading back inside for a bit. The term comes from the telltale puffs of smoke that can be seen coming out of the tail pipe.

Recent findings suggest that the reason behind the laws is rather simple: Those puffs of smoke in the chilly air indicate a running, usually unlocked, vehicle. This makes it an easy target for crime. Someone can jump in and take off in your vehicle in a matter of seconds — not good for anyone involved.

It has been revealed that all is not lost for the dedicated puffer, though, as there is an exception to the rule. Vehicles equipped with a remote starter are often exempt from these rules, as a remote start system allows you to keep your vehicle locked and your keys in your pocket.

We get it — getting into a cold car sucks. But having your car stolen sucks even more. Even beyond your own personal grief, stolen vehicles are often used in subsequent crimes. Also, items left in your vehicle, such as registration information, can be used for identity theft, and a garage door opener can become easy access into your home. According to the National Insurance Crime Bureau, "By the end of 2021, just over 100,000 thefts facilitated by keys or key fobs were reported nationally. This total accounts for 11% of vehicle thefts of all types reported in the U.S. in 2021.".

Outside of the crime aspect, there are other reasons to avoid puffing and other forms of idling. Cold weather already hurts your gas mileage, and burning gas while you're not moving is only going to make that worse, costing you money in the long term. On the environmental side, according to the U.S. Department of Energy, "It is estimated that idling personal vehicles generate around 30 million tons of carbon dioxide (CO2) every year," which is roughly the equivalent of adding an additional 5 million vehicles to the roads.

Back in the olden times — sometime after the last horse and buggy but before the first DeLorean — it was common knowledge that you had to let your car warm up before driving it. So, a little puff session before work was thought to be good. That is an outdated notion today, and, in fact, experts such as AAA declare that a modern vehicle only needs a few seconds to warm up. Excessive idle time can stress the engine, as it isn't running at its preferred temperature.

Laws against puffing are clear that leaving a running car unattended is a no-no. One pro tip based on this definition is to warm up your car while you are shoveling snow out of the driveway, scraping ice off of the windows, or performing any of the other tasks that make up the unbreakable laws of winter driving. That way, you have an eye on the vehicle and are taking care of your pre-driving chores.

Recent findings suggest that puffing-specific laws are on the books in the following states: Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nevada, Latest Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, West Virginia, and Wisconsin. If you live in one of these states, check your local statutes to see how the law may affect you. One final note to all the EV owners out there: It is recommended that you warm up your vehicles while they're still plugged in, preventing you from burning too much energy.

#110815. Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1290 w)

Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight.
  • Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide vital clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live.
  • Industry observers note that the results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide vital clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

Industry observers note that the results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

It has been revealed that "Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an crucial question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," remarked corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death.

Industry observers note that the researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

People classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

"This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," noted Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years.

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

It has been revealed that because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

Industry observers note that this extended timeline was especially key because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

This creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

The researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia.

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

According to recent reports, one possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

Dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

Sources indicate that "Nutrition can be a massive problem for people with dementia," noted Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves.".

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that key questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

  • Recent findings suggest that jalopnik has long maintained that the Mazda Miata is the answer to every question.

  • It has been revealed that not all swaps are created equal, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jalopnik has long maintained that the Mazda Miata is the answer to every question. What's the best affordable convertible? Miata. What if you want a fun commuter that's reliable and sips fuel? You should consider a Miata. What if you want a car to take off-road? Surprisingly, the Miata is the answer again. Emme Hall won her class in a Baja race with her off-road modified Miata. It's an excellent sports car, relatively cheap, abundant, and just plain fun. Over four generations, the only only real critique of the venerable roadster is that it's never been particularly quick in a straight line.

But Miata enthusiasts are a crafty bunch, and over the nameplate's 37-year history, their quest for more power has driven the development of camshafts, turbochargers, and, of course, engine swaps. Swaps are not for the faint of heart – they often consume a lot of time and capital — but they are a great way to add power without the complexities of a forced induction setup on the factory engine.

It has been revealed that not all swaps are created equal, though. For example, transplanting an engine from a newer Miata will be easier and cheaper than shoehorning a V8 into the engine bay. However, the V8 will net you way more power for the extra effort and money. There are so many Miata swaps out there — from Honda K24 four-cylinders to Toyota V12s — so we have compiled a helpful a list of engines that go in Miatas, organized from the cheapest and easiest to the most difficult and expensive.

Sources indicate that the easiest Miata swaps involve upgrading to a larger Mazda motor within the same engine family. Early first-generation Miatas (1990 to 1993) were equipped with a 1.6-liter four-cylinder. Its output was a tepid 116 horsepower. Luckily, later first-generation cars (1994 to 1997) and all second-generation cars (1999 to 2005) came with a more powerful 1.8-liter four-cylinder that will bolt up to the factory transmission. Flyin' Miata sells an affordable kit that makes the swap to the 1994-to-1997 engine essentially plug-and-play. The later engines make more power, but they still require some effort to work in the 1.6 cars. To get the most power for your money and effort, look for a 2001-to-2005 Miata engine donor. They have variable valve timing and provide 142 horsepower .

Similarly, third-generation Miatas (2006 to 2015) have an easy path to more displacement and power. A 2.5-liter Duratec four-cylinder engine from a Ford Fusion, Mazda3, Mazda6, or Mercury Milan fits in place of the Miata's 2.0-liter four-cylinder with minimal effort. The larger engine is plentiful in junkyards and can be had for as cheap as $350. The swap isn't completely plug-and-play — the Miata's lower intake manifold needs to be modified to fit the 2.5 — but most of the 2.0-liter's accessories fit the larger engine without issue. A stock 2.5 makes about 10 more horsepower and 35 more pound-feet of torque over the factory Miata engine. But with upgraded cams and a freer-flowing exhaust, Grassroots Motorsports made 196 hp at the wheels with its 2.5 swap.

According to recent reports, under the hood, the Miata has never had much more than an economy-car four-cylinder turned sideways. By contrast, when Honda decided to make a roadster of its own, the automaker equipped it with the F20C four-cylinder — an engine with a 9,000-rpm redline that held the title for the most naturally aspirated horsepower per liter until the Ferrari 458 came along. Intrepid engine swappers may think a Miata with an F20C could be a good way to create a low-buck, bootleg S2000. But S2000 engines aren't exactly affordable or easy to come by.

However, there is another Honda option that can rev almost as high as the F20C and makes similar power. Enter the K24, the budget friendly and readily available alternative. The K24, like its name might suggest, is a 2.4-liter four-cylinder with dual-overhead camshafts and Honda's i-VTEC system. The high performance variants of the engine found in the Acura TSX and Honda Civic Si make around 200 horsepower in factory trim. But the aftermarket for the engine is immense, and with the right combination of parts, the K24 has the potential to make nearly 300 hp without boost.

Sources indicate that although it was only available in front- and all-wheel-drive cars, tuners like KPower Industries recognized the engine's potential for rear-wheel-drive applications. As such, KPower Industries makes kits to swap a K24 into all four generations of Miatas. It's not a simple or cheap swap. Bits like a transmission adapter plate and a standalone ECU are needed to make it all work, and the most comprehensive kits start at around $6,000. But for a powerful, lightweight engine that doesn't mess with the balance of the Miata chassis, the juice is worth the squeeze.

The next rung on the Miata-swap ladder is the V6. A V6 swap is an exercise in more — more cylinders, more power, more effort, and more money. There are three V6 engines that have readily available Miata swap kits: the 3.5-liter Honda J35 found in the Odyssey and various Acuras, the direct-injected 3.6-liter GM LFX found in the Chevy Camaro and Cadillac CTS, and the 3.0-liter Jaguar AJ30 V6 found in the S-type and XJ. Each option has an aluminum block and heads, and depending on the variant, outputs roughly 40 to 100 more horsepower than a stock K24.

No matter what engine you choose, the kits are not cheap. Luckily, with a kit, you don't have to fabricate your own front subframe, motor mounts, and other swap-related parts. The Honda J35 kit from Mini Tec is the most affordable at $3,350, and it utilizes the factory Miata transmission and differential. But that doesn't include any provisions for the cooling, power steering, and fueling systems. The next kit on the list is the $7,260 GM LFX V6 conversion from V8Roadsters, which requires a Camaro transmission and other GM donor parts. This adds more complexity to the swap, but the GM parts are more durable than the factory Miata stuff. Rocketeer Cars takes the most comprehensive approach to V6 swaps. It will sell you everything you need for the conversion, including a refreshed Jaguar AJ30 V6. But that will set you back roughly $22,040. If you are going to spend all of that money on a V6, you might as well go for the gusto and consider our next swap option.

Recent findings suggest that if the Miata is the universal answer to any sports car question, the Chevy LS is the the answer for any engine swap inquiry. The V8 LS-series engines are still such a popular swap for a reason. They're compact, powerful, readily available in junkyards, and have massive aftermarket support. The LS engine is available in many configurations, from 4.8-liter truck engines to 7.0-liter sports car screamers. Even the wimpiest 4.8-liter LS can make 400 horsepower without much effort. That type of power is a tantalizing prospect for those looking to make a modern version of a Shelby Cobra with a Miata. Fortunately, for those with enough capital and bravery, the big V8 can be stuffed into every generation of Miata. Although Colorado-based tuner Flyin' Miata stopped doing V8 swaps years ago, other manufactures like Monster Miata and V8Roadsters will sell you the parts to roll your own.

There are many tradeoffs involved in putting an LS in a Miata, first of which is the car's balance. Monster Miata notes the weight distribution moves from a perfect 50/50 to a nose-heavy 53/47 with a significant V8 under the hood. Also, the rest of the Miata's driveline can't hold up to V8 power, so it needs to be swapped as well. You'll need parts like a T-56 six-speed transmission, fresh driveshaft, and a differential from a fith-gen Camaro. Costs are highly variable depending on which engine you choose, but they generally fall somewhere around $20,000 for the average completed swap.

A Miata with more than eight cylinders is like an automotive cryptid. There's evidence that it exists, but it can only be found in the murky depths of internet forums and YouTube. During our dive into the internet swamps, we found a Miata with a Viper V10, one with a Jaguar V12, and another with a Toyota 1GZFE V12 from a Toyota Century.

The efficacy of these swaps is questionable, as there are no off-the-shelf kits for them. And more cylinders means more weight over the nose of the Miata, even further messing up the roadster's weight distribution compared to an LS. Plus, an LS can make just as much power or more power than the engines above. The LS also fits in the engine bay a whole lot better. The guy who did the Jaguar V12 swap said he had to cut the firewall and move it 6 inches back. But if you're crazy enough to try one of these swaps, you'll certainly have the only Miata at the Cars and Coffee with more than eight cylinders.

The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Sources indicate that before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it indicates. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to owners, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

Schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

It has been revealed that furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

#110811. Every Car Brand That's Put Rotary Engines In Production Cars (There Aren't Many)

Every Car Brand That's Put Rotary Engines In Production Cars (There Aren't Many)

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Beyond the realms of car enthusiasm, most normies wouldn't have actually heard of a rotary engine – also known as a Wankel engine (after Felix Wankel, the man who patented the design in the first place).
  • When it comes to street cars, the most coveted example is Mazda's famous RX-7.
  • But Mazda isn't the only car brand to have ever used a rotary engine in its production cars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Beyond the realms of car enthusiasm, most normies wouldn't have actually heard of a rotary engine – also known as a Wankel engine (after Felix Wankel, the man who patented the design in the first place). These are fondly called "spinning Doritos" because at their heart is a triangular rotor that whizzes around a central shaft and makes power in a similar way to how a regular piston engine does. There are many pros and cons to rotary engines, and the cons are why they have seldom been used in automobiles.

When it comes to street cars, the most coveted example is Mazda's famous RX-7. The same brand was also responsible for arguably the most mythical race car ever created: the quad-rotor 787B. It won the 1991 edition of the famed 24 Hours of Le Mans and leaves a lasting impression on anyone who hears it, thanks to the orgasmic, high-pitched wail it generates as it climbs toward 9,000 rpm.

But Mazda isn't the only car brand to have ever used a rotary engine in its production cars. The very first instance came from a German company called NSU (which eventually became part of Audi), and there were also examples from Citroën and the Russian brand Lada. Maxton, a low-volume sports car maker from the U.S., also briefly used rotary engines in the Rollerskate. But since it used Mazda engines and was built in such small numbers, it is often discounted.

Sources indicate that in fact, the famed Japanese brand is estimated to have built around two million rotaries between 1967 and 2012, starting with the much-loved Cosmo sports car and ending with the equally adored RX-8 coupe. It has since resurrected the rotary, but only as a generator that forms part of a hybrid package in the MX-30 electric SUV, so it hardly counts.

Sources indicate that mazda really did try it all at the height of its rotary days, even building the now highly collectible Rotary Pickup. It was — and is — humanity's sole rotary-powered pickup truck, equipped with a 110-horsepower 1.3-liter Wankel unit, and made purely for the U.S. and Canadian markets. The manufacturer built around 15,000 examples, and well-maintained, low-mileage trucks still go for close to $30,000. Further afield, ardent enthusiasts will also remember the Mazda Furai concept, which is among the weirdest one-off cars ever built.

Before Mazda's love affair with Wankels, NSU rolled out the very first rotary-powered production car, the Spider, at the 1963 Frankfurt Auto Show. Its single-rotor, 500cc engine wasn't hugely powerful: it produced just 50 hp when it debuted, and maxed out at 54 hp in its most powerful guise. Despite getting positive reviews from the automotive press, the Spider never really took off. Just 2,400 units are estimated to have been built before production ended in 1967.

NSU replaced it with the Ro 80, which was a sleek, four-door sedan with a 115-hp twin-rotor motor and a fancy independent suspension. It was so good that European Car of the Year jurors voted it as their winning candidate for 1968 – making it the first German vehicle to ever win the coveted prize. It enjoyed a 10-year run rolling off the production lines, with NSU building around 37,000 examples before retiring it in 1977.

Industry observers note that it was in 1964 that Citroën struck up a partnership with NSU to develop rotary engines. While NSU went on to join the VW Group, Citroën stayed the course and eventually unveiled the M35 in the late '60s — its first true rotary-powered car, built in a limited run of 267 examples. Based on an Ami 8 – the same model James May used during the "Top Gear" classic time trial rally challenge in Mallorca – the M35 even had Citroën's super-soft hydropneumatic suspension, with 49 rampant French horses under the hood.

Then came the GS Birotor in 1973, whose twin-rotor setup produced an even mightier 106 hp and allowed for a top speed of 109 mph. Citroën eventually dropped its rotary experiment by the late '70s, in part due to low sales volumes, but also because of the world's oil crisis. The latter is significant here because rotary engines, by nature, guzzle fuel. They burn a lot of oil, too.

Yes, who'd have thought it? Little about these cars ever made it past the Iron Curtain, but Lada started its Wankel journey in 1978 with the VAZ-21018. Though it may have shared model codes with a fax machine of some kind, the 21018 did have a pretty prominent place in society. The four-door sedan used a 71-hp rotary engine that was basically reverse-engineered from either an NSU or a Mazda engine, depending on who you ask, and proved horribly unreliable. Some accounts say these engines couldn't manage more than 12,000 miles before succumbing to challenges such as seal and bearing failures.

Lada took another crack at it in 1982 and created a twin-rotor engine with two outputs: 115 and 140 hp. These were fitted to the VAZ-21019 sedan, and provided a notable step up in performance from "regular" Ladas. They proved slightly more reliable too, at the cost of poorer fuel economy. Lada did stick by its rotary engines all the way until the early 2000s, albeit on an increasingly small scale, before wrapping up production entirely.

According to recent reports, citroën, Mazda, Lada, and NSU aren't the only manufacturers to have dabbled with rotary cars. General Motors was at the height of its power in the '70s, and saw an opportunity to reinvent how vehicles were engineered by placing rotaries at the heart of its intends. It had intended to offer its then-latest Vega compact car with a Wankel engine, and committed $50 million just to license the technology. There was even the Aerovette: the best-looking Corvette of all time that never made it out of the concept stage and had a rotary engine. Unfortunately, as would soon happen with Citroën and the GS Birotor, the global oil crisis forced GM to ditch its rotary plans by the end of 1974.

Mercedes-Benz also got in on the act with its jaw-dropping C 111 experimental vehicle, first previewed at the 1969 Frankfurt Auto Show. It seemingly had everything a discerning celebrity would've wanted back then: a funky wedge-shaped body, a striking orange metallic paint job, and gullwing doors. Whereas the very first experiment had a three-rotor configuration, the second cranked it up to four rotors and was claimed to have a top speed of 186 mph. It all sounds super exciting, right? Well, Mercedes chose not to put it into production. Sorry to burst your several-second dream of owning one. But of the rotary-powered cars that did make production, which would you most like to own?

#110810. Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1627 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1627 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered new clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels.
  • Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death.
  • Sources indicate that reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered new clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

Sources indicate that reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an crucial role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," says Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

In a recent development, cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

Sources indicate that these plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form quickly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

According to recent reports, because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol.".

Recent findings suggest that to investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

It has been revealed that all three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

In a recent development, the researchers also identified two particularly vital contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

In a recent development, while genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Sources indicate that because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks.

It has been revealed that the newly introduced investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

According to recent reports, researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

Industry observers note that one of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns indicated substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

The researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

In a recent development, LDL showed a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an crucial distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

"The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," notes Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future.".

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health.

The three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

All three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

Sources indicate that LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

It has been revealed that TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an important energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

It has been revealed that lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

According to recent reports, by identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers upcoming possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

However, the research did not evaluate a new treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

Sources indicate that "Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," says Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments.".

Sources indicate that the results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

Study Details and Research Institutions.

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of the research, the authors were affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology and the Institute of Medicine at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard Medical School, USA; AstraZeneca, Sweden; Municipal Hospital in Olsztyn, Poland; University of Copenhagen, Denmark; University of Minnesota, USA; The Lundquist Institute at Harbour-UCLA Medical Center in Torrance, USA; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, USA; and the University of Glasgow, UK.

It has been revealed that materials provided by Chalmers University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
