💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.
  • The company reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents.
  • The results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:33 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Elastic N.V.’s stock was trending lower in late trading today after the enterprise search software firm reported earnings and revenue that beat Wall Street’s expectations but disappointed with guidance that came in below forecasts.

The company reported second-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of 94 cents per share, easily beating the analyst consensus estimate of 81 cents. Revenue rose 17%, to $496 million, surpassing the Street’s target of $487 million.

The results helped Elastic bounce back into profitability. Its net income for the quarter came to $171 million, rebounding from a loss of $51.3 million in the same period one year ago.

However, investors were less than impressed with the company’s guidance. For the quarter in progress, Elastic said it’s looking for earnings of between 90 cents and 92 cents per share on sales of $507.5 million to $508.5 million. That’s some way below the Street’s targets of 95 cents in earnings and $517.6 million in revenue. The company is not helped by the weak Euro, with currency conversions likely to cause a $4.5 million headwind on revenue in the quarter.

The full-year picture is not much better, as Elastic forecast annual sales of between $2 billion and $2.01 billion compared with the Street’s model of $2.01 billion.

Sources indicate that netherlands-based Elastic is one of Europe’s most successful software companies. It’s the developer of the popular open-source enterprise search platform Elasticsearch, which is used by thousands of businesses all over the world. The base platform is free to download and use, with Elastic making money by selling a special cloud-hosted version that ships with premium features not available in the open edition. The organization also sells application observability and security tools.

Recent findings suggest that in the last couple of years, Elastic has tried to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom by positioning Elasticsearch as a useful cog in the wheel that feeds real-time data into large language models to provide them with business context. A key capability is Elastic Context Engine, which gathers, structures, and serves business-specific context to AI agents so they can make accurate decisions with fewer tokens and lower latency.

More recently, the company has built AI-native products including AlertZero, which enables enterprises to orchestrate teams of autonomous security agents that automate tasks around data protection and threat hunting.

In a recent development, elastic Chief Executive Ash Kulkarni (pictured) said he’s excited about the potential of those upcoming capabilities to drive significant revenue over time. “Elastic delivered another strong quarter, beating guidance across all key metrics,” he said. “Our strong results reflect expanding customer adoption and position us well to continue our strong execution in the back half of fiscal 2027.”.

In a recent development, unfortunately for Kulkarni, investors didn’t seem to share his enthusiasm. The market was clearly expecting trouble on the horizon in the hours before the firm published its report, as its stock declined 8% during regular trading. Once the results were out, it fell another 8% after-hours. That means Elastic’s stock is now up just over 1% in the year to date.

Elastic’s stock had rallied more than 150% between April and October, but virtually all of those gains have now been erased. Prior to today, the shares had already lost more than 20% this month amid broader concerns about the AI industry. Some investors continue to worry about the potential of AI technology to challenge the business models of software companies.

Elastic is trying to sidestep those concerns by de-emphasizing search and observability and moving towards runtime context, model evaluation and AI operations, but investors are not yet convinced it will be able to do so successfully, Constellation Research analyst Michael Ni told SiliconANGLE.

“While Elastic is showing good underlying momentum, the Street wants to see more proof that its re-acceleration can hold,” Ni mentioned. “The next few quarters will show whether the broader platform story translates into sustainable growth or remains ahead of the numbers.”.

Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Industry observers note that the U.S. Department of Labor proposed fresh policy this week that would end fast-track green cards for healthcare professionals like nurses and physical therapists—the latest in a string of policies from the Trump administration raising the bar for foreign-born workers and students across healthcare and other industries.

It has been revealed that presently, nurses, physical therapists and other workers “with exceptional ability in the sciences or arts” are granted an exemption from an administrative test in the permanent labor certification program (PERM), a months-long administrative process in which an employer must prove there are no able, willing, qualified and available U.S. workers for a permanent job ahead of sponsoring a foreign worker.

In a recent development, the exemption, referred to Schedule A, is given to occupations where the DOL recognizes a nationwide shortage of U.S. workers. Nurses and physical therapists have been listed under Schedule A for more than 30 years.

The Department of Labor, in its newly proposed rule, stated it wants to eliminate Schedule A as it cannot “demonstrate that the occupations right now listed in Schedule A are still shortage occupations.”.

Industry observers note that it cited in the proposed rule a late 2023 request for information published under the Biden administration seeking input on potentially expanding Schedule A. Despite more than 2,000 responses, DOL now claims it didn’t receive the information it would need to establish a methodology for regularly reviewing and updating Schedule A occupations, and questioned whether it has the statutory authority to make such occupational exemptions in the first place.

“The elimination of Schedule A would enable the Department to better ensure that U.S. workers have an opportunity to apply for available job opportunities, and adhere to the statutory requirements to protect U.S. workers assigned to it, as intended by Congress under the [Immigration and Nationality Act].”.

The proposed rule, which is open to public comment for 60 days, also includes requirements for employers to advertise their open jobs more broadly and for a longer period of time to demonstrate a good-faith effort to recruit American workers before turning to a green card sponsorship. These and other proposed changes would be the first “comprehensive” reforms to the PERM program in almost two decades, the Department of Labor remarked.

If finalized as-is, employers who want to sponsor professional nurses, physical therapists and other affected roles “would be required to go through the lengthier and costlier PERM labor market testing process, adding time, cost and administrative work to a pathway that hospitals, nursing homes and rehabilitation providers have historically relied on to fill persistent shortages,” Caroline Tang, an Austin shareholder at labor and employment law firm Ogletree Deakins, told Fierce Healthcare.

It has been revealed that industry associations as well as other sections of the government have widely projected shortages in the healthcare workforce, including nurses, for the coming years. The Heart Resources and Services Association’s National Center for Health Workforce Analysis, for instance, projects (PDF) national shortages of registered nurses through at least 2038, with a projected 8% shortage in 2028 that is more severe in non-metro areas.

The proposed policy change is among several brought by the Trump administration in line with an order from the White House to prioritize domestic hiring—though many have been stymied in the courts.

Among the most prominent is a $100,000 supplemental fee the Department of Homeland Security attached to H-1B petitions that was vacated by two separate judged, and in August was succeeded by the somewhat altered proposal of an additional H-1B petition fee of $103,265. Another policy from the same department tightening how long nonimmigrant students may remain in the country (referred to as “duration of status”) was temporary blocked hours before implementation in September and fully vacated on Monday (PDF), though the former decision is already being appealed.

The Department of Labor has also proposed increasing the prevailing wage floors for several green cards that legal experts expect will be challenged by employers that would shoulder the resulting financial burden.

UnitedHealthcare is teaming up with CPSEN for a upcoming program that will lean on community pharmacists to reach Medicaid patients.

The insurance giant remarked Wednesday that its through the UHC Pharmacy Care Hub model, pharmacists will work alongside the payer's care managers and providers to help close gaps in care and support management for chronic conditions and other needs.

Participating pharmacies will offer a range of services, including telehealth, medication management, point-of-care testing and personalized supports. The program is built on a hub-and-spoke model, where pharmacists can then help lead the patient to the right site of care or through any follow-up if needed.

These interactions can also help track patterns in emergency care use, and help patients find a more appropriate setting if their needs aren't emergent.

Industry observers note that the program is currently available to UnitedHealthcare Medicaid members in seven states: Florida, Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. UHC expects to add additional states throughout the year.

Part of the goal, the company stated, is to tap into the trust that local pharmacists have in the communities they serve.

Recent findings suggest that “Community pharmacies are trusted, local access points for care,” noted Arethusa Kirk, M.D., chief medical officer for UnitedHealthcare Community & State, in the announcement. “This newly introduced model expands the services independent pharmacists can help deliver, making it easier for people—especially those facing barriers to care—to get timely support closer to home.”.

UHC noted that most (89%) of Americans live within five miles of a pharmacy, making these locations an easier option to access for many. This is especially true for individuals who may struggle to find an appointment with a doctor or find transportation to a visit.

In a recent development, for example, a participating pharmacist in North Carolina, Madeline Clark, remarked in the announcement that a patient came into the pharmacy for a urine test, as she had a potential urinary tract infection. The pharmacy conducted the test and sent the results virtually to a provider through UnitedHealthcare's Doctor Chat tool.

A prescription was then filled for the patient in the same visit, and she was out the door within about 30 minutes.

Clark noted the patient was thankful not just for the ease of that trip to the pharmacy but for avoiding a visit to the ER as well.

"Not only was this a lower cost of care in the healthcare system space, but it also was just incredibly helpful for the patient," she remarked.

Tech Report: Common forever chemicals linked to nearly double the rate of aggressive breast cancer

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to new research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S.
  • The study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS).
  • Industry observers note that both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that women with higher blood levels of two common "forever chemicals" may face an increased risk of developing a particularly aggressive form of breast cancer, according to new research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH), part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).

The study identified a connection between estrogen receptor-negative, or ER-negative, breast cancer and two widely encountered chemicals: perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). Women with greater concentrations of these substances in their blood were more likely to develop this type of cancer. However, researchers found no clear link between either chemical and breast cancer risk overall.

Industry observers note that both substances belong to a large family of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly called PFAS. These chemicals have been used in numerous everyday consumer products and are often described as "forever chemicals" because they resist breaking down in the environment. They can also accumulate in the human body and remain there for years.

"Women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health," mentioned HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. "This NIH study links two forever chemicals to a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer and demands further investigation. Under President Trump's leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks, and give women the information they need to protect their health.".

Why This Aggressive Breast Cancer Is Concerning.

ER-negative breast cancer differs from more common forms of the disease because its tumor cells lack the receptors that allow estrogen to stimulate cancer growth. These cancers are often more aggressive and generally have poorer outcomes than tumors that respond to estrogen.

Despite their severity, researchers still have relatively little information about what makes someone more likely to develop ER-negative breast cancer. The new findings suggest that exposure to certain persistent environmental chemicals could be one contributing factor.

"Our findings, which we confirmed using a meta-analysis of prior research, indicate that certain legacy PFAS, including PFOA and PFOS, are associated with a higher risk of ER-negative breast cancer, a more aggressive tumor type with few known risk factors," explained NIH Stadtman Investigator Alexandra White, Ph.D., who led the study.

The findings were published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.

Higher Forever Chemical Levels Linked to Greater Cancer Risk.

Industry observers note that to investigate the possible connection, NIH scientists and their collaborators examined blood samples that had been collected years before participants received a cancer diagnosis. The researchers measured concentrations of 17 different PFAS chemicals, allowing them to compare earlier exposure levels with subsequent breast cancer outcomes.

The results revealed substantial differences for two chemicals. Women in the highest PFOA exposure group had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer than women in the lowest group. The association was even stronger for PFOS, with the highest exposure group showing a 93% higher rate, nearly twice that of the lowest group.

These percentages represent relative differences between groups rather than the absolute probability that an individual woman will develop breast cancer. The findings also establish an association, not proof that the chemicals directly cause the disease.

The analysis used data from the Sister Study, a major research project conducted by NIH's National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (NIEHS). Between 2003 and 2009, the study enrolled 50,884 women ages 35-74 from across the United States and Puerto Rico.

All participants were free of breast cancer when they enrolled, although each had a full or half-sister who had already been diagnosed with the disease. For the PFAS investigation, researchers analyzed information from 1,609 women who subsequently developed breast cancer and a comparison group of 2,269 women.

Could Reducing PFAS Exposure Lower Cancer Risk?

In a recent development, although PFAS can remain in the environment and the body for long periods, researchers emphasize that exposure is not necessarily unavoidable. The findings could eventually help identify newly introduced ways to reduce the risk of aggressive breast cancer.

"These findings matter for women's health broadly," stated first author, Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., who previously worked as an NIH research fellow and is now a researcher at DLH, a scientific research organization. "Although PFAS are persistent in the environment and in our bodies, exposure to them is still potentially modifiable, meaning people can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open fresh avenues for prevention.".

It has been revealed that the researchers are also interested in understanding how these chemicals might influence cancer development. Because the strongest associations appeared in tumors that lack estrogen receptors, the findings suggest that PFAS could act through biological processes unrelated to hormonal signaling.

Industry observers note that potential explanations include changes in gene activity or alterations in the immune system. However, the study did not directly investigate these mechanisms, so their involvement remains uncertain.

Newer Forever Chemicals Raise Unanswered Questions.

Sources indicate that although PFOA and PFOS have largely been phased out and replaced with other PFAS compounds, measurable amounts of both substances are still present in most people's bodies. Their persistence means that exposure to these older chemicals remains a potential public health concern.

The researchers say additional investigations should focus on populations with greater PFAS exposure, as well as groups that experience higher rates of ER-negative breast cancer. Such research could help clarify the strength of the observed associations and identify whether certain populations face greater risks.

Scientists also need to determine whether the newer chemicals introduced as replacements for PFOA and PFOS carry similar health concerns.

"More research is needed, particularly evaluating the risk of breast cancer associated with newer replacement PFAS chemicals," White said.

The findings add to growing questions about the long-term health effects of forever chemicals and highlight the importance of understanding how environmental exposures may contribute to aggressive forms of breast cancer.

The research received support from NIEHS grants Z01ES044005; Z1AES103332; and R01ES032831.

A real-life Barbie dream house is turning heads in Hudson, WI, where an eye-catching pink Victorian has gone under contract after hitting the market for $1.1 million in June 2026.

With its pink walkway, bubble gum–colored staircase, and vibrant interior, this seven-bedroom, 5,189-square-foot home is anything but ordinary.

But behind its playful Barbie-inspired appearance is a spacious historical residence built in 1900 that is packed with character, original details, and incredible versatility.

In a recent development, “An everyday buyer interested in a classic Victorian home might think this is a bit much,” says listing agent Jennifer R. Martin of Edina Realty Inc. “It has a lot of great qualities. I would say to anyone not to let the color deter you. Painting is easy, and it’s not that expensive to make changes.”.

Recent findings suggest that presently a successful short-term rental, the home is near the St. Croix River and could be used for multigenerational living or converted into a single-family home.

According to recent reports, “The sizing alone of the house is incredible,” Martin says. “It’s enormous and goes on forever. It has two separate kitchens, so it could also be turned into a duplex.”.

It is part of a collection of rose-hued homes operated by Fleetwood Rentals, which hosts everything from birthday parties to bachelorette weekends.

In a recent development, “The seller’s clientele is looking for a party weekend destination,” she notes. “It’s one block from the riverfront and two blocks away from downtown.”.

Located 30 minutes from the Minneapolis/St. Paul airport, the property last changed hands for $614,000 in 2020. It offers “outstanding income potential,” the listing states.

“When the seller bought it, right away she had it painted in dark charcoal,” Martin states. “Her vision at that time was to have a Goth mansion that would be similar to Disney’s Haunted Mansion. It was right around the time the 'Barbie' movie was coming out, so she decided to take advantage of that.”.

In a recent development, the multilevel home also has formal and casual dining spaces and expansive gathering areas. Original details include woodwork, built-in cabinetry, vaulted ceilings, and dual staircases.

"I envisioned the next buyer to be either another Airbnb owner or a large family who would un-pinkify it," Martin says with a laugh. "It's a great house with a lot of great qualities. I told potential buyers not to let the color deter you.".

Recent findings suggest that the living room has pink walls, drapes, and couches. The formal dining room has built-in cabinetry and a fireplace. The light-filled kitchen, with an enormous breakfast bar, is a surprise with its white cabinetry and a copper farmhouse sink.

Industry observers note that the bubble gum–painted grand staircase leads to the colorful sleeping quarters. Four bedrooms are on the second level and three more are on the third floor. The primary suite has a walk-in closet, a soaking tub, a separate glass shower, and a dual-sink vanity.

Other highlights include a home theater, a hot tub, a 14-foot swim spa, and a patio designed for entertaining. The fenced lot comes with a private patio, a two-car garage, and a driveway with parking for 12 vehicles.

The property is conveniently located near boutique shopping, riverfront parks, and the marina.

"Hudson is a riverfront town with tons of history," Martin claims. "People love to come here for bachelorette parties and places to go out to dinner. It also has a lot of charming, fun shops.".

Aetna unveils new program aimed at offering end-to-end support for moms and babies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Aetna is rolling out a upcoming program that aims to provide key end-to-end care for pregnant women, new mothers and infants.

The offering, called Aetna For You and Baby, will be available to all expectant mothers enrolled in an Aetna plan. Through the program, moms will be connected to a prenatal visit in their first trimester and a postpartum visit within 12 weeks of the baby's birth.

Women in the program will also be screened for depression both during and after pregnancy to identify any risks.

In addition to supporting the mother both during pregnancy and postpartum, the program aims to give babies a healthy start by providing at least six well visits through their first 15 months, which offer critical tests and screenings, checkups and vaccinations.

The news of the launch was provided first to Fierce Healthcare.

Katerina Guerraz, Aetna's chief operating officer, told Fierce that maternal care often focuses mostly, if not completely, on labor and delivery, though prenatal and postpartum visits play a critical role in driving positive health outcomes.

In its announcement, Aetna notes that data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that about 90% of pregnancy-related deaths could have been prevented, with a lack of access to prenatal care and more complete support making for a key barrier.

"This is a national access issue, a quality issue, and it's an affordability problem," she noted.

In addition, it's not uncommon for programs that aim to drive better maternal outcomes to lack services for the babies, who in the first year of life undergo a wide array of critical developmental milestones, Guerraz mentioned.

In a recent development, aetna, as the third-largest insurer in the U.S., sees about 200,000 deliveries a year among its members. That means the success of this program could have a significant impact in a short amount of time, supporting at least 1 million babies over the next five years, she mentioned.

Aetna for You and Baby also builds on a broader push within the manufacturer to build a more personalized and simple experience for members. For instance, the company established a program that embeds Aetna nurses in the hospital to support discharge planning and transitions for members, and Guerraz said that holds potential in the maternal care space.

For example, if a baby needs to stay in the neonatal intensive care unit after birth, having an Aetna nurse in the NICU providing additional support to the clinical team and the member would pay dividends, she said.

Aetna is also plugged into Health 100, a sister subsidiary of its parent company, CVS Health, that offers an AI-powered tool to help patients identify healthcare costs and navigate their benefits, even if they're not members of Aetna or Caremark or CVS Pharmacy customers.

Guerraz mentioned the program is designed to offer something that patients can carry with them if their coverage changes.

She added that the team intends to continue iterating on the program and identifying other barriers to care for moms and their babies.

"This is something that we know is going to have a massive impact," she said.

Stopping statins after 70 may be safer than expected, but there's a catch

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A major new study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks.
  • Industry observers note that the independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago.
  • An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A major new study suggests that many adults age 70 and older who have never experienced a heart attack or stroke may be able to stop taking statins without substantially increasing their short-term cardiovascular risks. However, the findings also point to a possible increase in risk over a longer period, making the decision more complicated than it initially appears.

Industry observers note that the independent, preliminary research was presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held November 6 through 9 in Chicago. The annual conference brings together cardiovascular researchers and healthcare professionals from around the world to share scientific discoveries, emerging evidence, and advances in clinical care.

An estimated 25% of American adults have elevated levels of low-density lipoprotein-cholesterol (LDL-C), commonly called "bad cholesterol." When too much LDL cholesterol accumulates in the arteries, it can restrict blood flow and contribute to heart attacks and strokes. Statins are widely prescribed to lower cholesterol and reduce these risks, including in people who have never experienced a cardiovascular event. This preventive approach remains a central part of the American Heart Association's 2026 joint guideline on dyslipidemia.

Do Older Adults Need to Keep Taking Statins?

Although statins are an established treatment for reducing cardiovascular risk, questions remain about how much benefit they provide when people reach their 70s and beyond, particularly if they have never had a heart attack or stroke.

"While the Association's recent joint guideline recommends lifestyle and potentially medication for people with high LDL-C at younger ages to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, recent studies question the health benefits of continuing statins in the later decades of life," remarked study author Rita F. Redberg, M.D., M.Sc., FAHA, professor of cardiology and the Araxe Vilensky Endowed Chair in Cardiology at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine. "A few previous studies assessed the safety of discontinuing statins for primary prevention at age 70 and later, and they found no difference in mortality. One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins. Whether it is safe to discontinue statins to prevent a first CVD event in the elderly remained unclear and the question we explored in our study.".

In a recent development, to investigate, researchers enrolled nearly 1,900 adults aged 70 and older who were taking statins specifically to prevent a first cardiovascular event. Every participant also had at least two chronic medical conditions, such as a history of cancer or lung disease.

Participants were divided into two groups. One group stopped taking statins, while the other continued their prescribed treatment. Researchers tracked their health for approximately two years, with additional follow-up extending as long as four years. They examined rates of heart attack, stroke, and death, along with changes in quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and muscle wasting (known as sarcopenia).

What Happened When Older Adults Stopped Statins?

The initial findings were largely reassuring. After approximately two years, participants who stopped taking statins did not experience a statistically significant increase in heart attacks, strokes, or deaths compared with those who remained on the medications.

Stopping treatment also did not produce measurable improvements in the other outcomes researchers examined. Quality of life, muscle discomfort, falls, and muscle wasting were similar in both groups.

There was, however, a small difference in cardiovascular outcomes. Over the first two years, the results indicated approximately one additional cardiovascular event for every 40 people who discontinued statins compared with those who continued treatment.

Industry observers note that the longer follow-up revealed a more concerning pattern. Over a period of up to four years, 12.7% of participants who stopped statins experienced a heart attack, stroke, or death, compared with 9.2% of those who kept taking the medications.

Longer Follow-Up Reveals a Potential Risk.

Sources indicate that redberg explained that the higher rate of serious outcomes during the four-year follow-up represents a newly introduced finding in research on statin discontinuation among older adults. She suggested that the difference may have emerged because this trial included more participants and tracked them for a longer period than earlier studies.

These results complicate the question of whether older adults should continue cholesterol treatment indefinitely. While the findings suggest that stopping statins may be a reasonable option for many people in this age group, they also indicate that remaining on treatment could offer some protection over time.

"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," she said. "There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event.".

Study Design and Crucial Limitations.

According to recent reports, the trial involved 1,880 participants aged 70 and older (average age of 77; 53% men, and 47% women), all of whom had at least two chronic health conditions. Individuals with established cardiovascular disease or a previous cardiovascular event were not eligible to participate.

Researchers conducted the study between November 2021 and April 2026 across 24 medical centers in Switzerland, France, and the Netherlands. Of the participants, 938 were assigned to discontinue statins, while 942 were assigned to continue taking their medications.

Throughout the trial and subsequent follow-up, researchers recorded heart attacks, acute ischemic strokes, and deaths from any cause. Participants also completed surveys assessing their overall quality of life, muscle pain, falls, and sarcopenia.

Recent findings suggest that one limitation was that some participants did not remain in their originally assigned groups. Some people instructed to stop statins eventually resumed treatment, while others assigned to continue taking statins stopped using them. Altogether, approximately 14% of participants switched from their assigned treatment approach during the study.

To determine whether these changes affected the findings, the researchers performed several additional statistical analyses. The results remained unchanged.

In a recent development, taken together, the findings suggest that discontinuing statins may be an option for many adults over 70 who have not previously experienced cardiovascular disease, especially when considering outcomes over the first two years. However, the higher rate of heart attacks, strokes, and deaths during longer follow-up underscores why stopping treatment should be an individualized decision made with a healthcare professional rather than a general recommendation for all older adults.

Healthcare purchasers must weigh hospital quality alongside their prices, Leapfrog claims" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Patient safety watchdog The Leapfrog Group released its latest collection of hospital safety grades hand-in-hand with calls for policymakers and stakeholders to consider, or directly tie patient safety reporting to price transparency.

The twice-yearly release brought top marks for 900 out of a total 2,366 graded hospitals, and the lowest “F” score for just three. There were 774 hospitals that earned a “B” grade, 655 a “C” grade, and 35 a “D” grade.

It has been revealed that no grades were assigned to another 447 hospitals, a decision the group made after a judge’s ruling in a lawsuit involving the scores it would assign to facilities that did not voluntarily submit their quality data to Leapfrog’s survey (Leapfrog appealed that decision in September). Leapfrog’s decision not to score these has generally shifted its letter grade distribution upward, and the organization has stated it is reviewing a potential methodology change for upcoming gradings to incorporate non-submitting hospitals.

Still, “a record number of hospitals are choosing to publicly report their safety and quality performance, and we applaud them for holding themselves accountable to their patients,” Leapfrog President and CEO Leah Binder mentioned in a statement.

According to recent reports, at the state level, Connecticut maintained its claim on the largest portion of hospitals earning an “A” grade (64.3% of its total), followed by Utah, New Jersey and South Carolina. Leapfrog also called out Rhode Island and Maine for jumping up the rankings—from eighteenth to seventh for the former, and from seventeenth to eighth for the latter. No hospitals were given an “A” grade in five states: Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota, Vermont and Wyoming.

Recent findings suggest that A hospital’s assigned grade is calculated by reviewing recent data on up to 22 patient safety measures, including a 10-part Medicare composite of reported patient safety and adverse events. Safety scores for specific hospitals can be searched on the group’s website.

Leapfrog and Binder, in a news release outlining its latest scores, made the case that its grades and similar independent measures warrant a seat at the table in a transparency conversation primarily focused on hospital costs.

“Progress on price transparency is vital, but there’s no good price for bad care,” Binder remarked. “We are calling on the Trump Administration and Congress to ensure price transparency is integrated with patient safety and quality transparency.”.

Recent findings suggest that the group backed its calls by pointing to a recent analysis (PDF) conducted by the Purchaser Business Group on Health (PBGH) that reviewed employer claims, federal price transparency data, and quality and safety measures including Leapfrog’s. It “found little to no correlation between negotiated prices and standardized quality measures,” as hospitals that received high safety grades often charged cheaper prices than those in the same market with lower grades.

Leapfrog and Elizabeth Mitchell, president and CEO of PBGH, noted the analysis—currently being expanded for practical usage by healthcare purchasers—is an example of how a more wholistic view of prices and care delivery should be considered when weighing a hospital.

It has been revealed that “Employers have an appropriate duty to pay a fair price for high-quality care, and they can’t meet it by looking at price alone,” Mitchell stated in the release from Leapfrog. “When we put the data together, some of the most expensive hospitals were not the safest. Our members want to buy high-quality, safe care that is fairly priced. That shouldn’t be too much to ask.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:41 EST / NOVEMBER 19 2026.

Google LLC today released a new version of Gemini’s Mac client that can interact with other apps on the user’s computer.

Industry observers note that the feature is available in the U.S. on launch. It requires a Google AI subscription, which equips consumer Google accounts with a broader lineup of artificial intelligence tools. The offering also includes additional storage space and certain other features.

Industry observers note that customers can instruct Gemini to launch a local app by including the command “@Computer use” in their prompts. For example, a designer could upload a sketch of a vehicle and ask the AI assistant to turn it into a three-dimensional animation. Gemini finds the local app that is needed for the task, creates a project blueprint and carries out the work step by step.

The assistant supports tasks that comprise dozens of actions. Furthermore, consumers can use the output of a newly completed Gemini workflow to launch follow-up projects. A user could have the assistant generate a visual asset in a design tool and then turn it into a mini-app with Visual Studio Code.

In a recent development, gemini can interact with not only local apps but also web services. That means it can load data from webpages into programs that run on the user’s machine, as well as move data in the opposite direction and between cloud services.

In a recent development, the AI carries out its work in a background window. As a result, consumers don’t have to pause their work while the assistant is running. They can track Gemini workflows via a preview pane built into the Mac client’s chat window. Additionally, Google has included controls that make it possible to give Gemini feedback mid-task.

“Privacy and safety are built in: you choose which apps Gemini can access, watch every step live, pause at any time, and approve key actions before they happen,” Michael Friedman, Google’s group product manager for the Gemini app, wrote in a blog post.

The Mac version of Muse, Meta Platforms Inc.’s recently introduced AI agent, can also interact with local apps and data. Furthermore, a cloud-based virtual machine enables it to perform tasks even when the user’s computer is offline. Dots, a competing service from OpenAI Group PBC, offers a similar capability.

In a recent development, google may seek to match its rivals’ cloud-based workflow hosting features in the future. The company can also extend Gemini in other ways. Notably, it could bring Gemini’s computer use mode to additional operating systems and add features for business customers. OpenAI’s Dots already includes capabilities designed to automate business workflows such as procurement.

#110736. Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

📅 14 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1011 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1011 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A smile might brighten your mood, but new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect.
  • For years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier.
  • According to recent reports, "I used to work in customer service.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A smile might brighten your mood, but new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect. When smiling becomes an obligation, especially one tied to financial pressure, it may actually leave people feeling less happy and more irritated.

For years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier. Yet those findings never quite matched his own experiences.

According to recent reports, "I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida," laughed Coles, a professor of psychology at the University of Florida. "So I'm looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world.".

It has been revealed that that contradiction inspired Coles and his colleagues to investigate what happens when people must keep smiling, rather than simply trying it once. Their findings suggest an important distinction: A brief, intentional smile can provide a small emotional lift, but repeatedly putting on a smile under pressure can undermine happiness.

Testing How Forced Smiling Affects Happiness.

According to recent reports, to explore this difference, Coles worked with researchers Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi to design an experiment that more closely resembled the demands of customer service jobs. Their findings were published on October 1 in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

It has been revealed that "We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren't successfully smiling," Coles said. "We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile.".

According to recent reports, the online experiment initially enrolled 1,201 people, with data from 1,174 included in the final analysis. Participants were shown images designed to produce different emotional reactions. Some depicted appealing subjects, such as kittens and flowers, while others revealed disturbing situations, including theft and mistreatment of animals.

Recent findings suggest that during the experiment, participants either deliberately formed a smile or allowed their facial expressions to develop naturally. Depending on their assigned group, they completed the exercise once or repeated it 10 times.

In a recent development, to introduce an element of pressure, researchers warned half the participants that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 from their $6 payment. However, nobody actually lost any money, and every participant received the full amount.

When Fake Smiles Start to Backfire.

Industry observers note that after completing each task, participants reported how happy they felt. The results showed that the emotional effects of smiling depended on how often people had to do it and whether they felt pressured.

In a recent development, when participants viewed unpleasant images, producing a single smile gave their mood a modest boost. This benefit appeared even among those who had been warned about a possible financial penalty. However, the positive effect weakened when smiling was repeated, and it disappeared when repeated smiles were combined with the threat of losing money.

The pattern was even more revealing when people looked at pleasant pictures. Smiling just once offered little additional happiness compared with allowing their faces to respond naturally. But when participants had to smile repeatedly or felt pressure to do so, their happiness ratings actually fell below those of people who responded naturally.

Further analysis revealed another unexpected consequence. In the pleasant picture conditions, forced smiling was also associated with increased irritation and anger.

"If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right," he said. "But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don't do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse.".

The Hidden Emotional Cost of Smiling at Work.

These findings may help explain why expectations to appear cheerful throughout the workday can become frustrating rather than uplifting.

Industry observers note that the problem has already sparked controversy in the workplace. In recent years, Target faced widespread criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Although the policy was intended to encourage friendly interactions, Coles argues that such requirements can interfere with people's ability to express their emotions naturally.

Industry observers note that the problem may extend beyond employees. Customers can also feel obligated to respond positively to friendliness that is being imposed rather than offered spontaneously. According to Coles, these expectations limit the emotional freedom of both sides of the interaction.

Could Trying Less to Be Happy Make Us Happier?

In a recent development, after spending years investigating how people can improve their emotional well-being, Coles has begun considering a broader question. Rather than constantly searching for ways to increase happiness, might people be better off placing greater value on simply being content?

His research suggests that efforts to manufacture positive emotions do not always produce the intended results. Sometimes, trying too hard to appear happy can make the experience less pleasant.

"As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we at the moment are," he mentioned, "much less emphasis on just being content with what we have.".

Materials provided by University of Florida. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act.
  • Senate committee leaders Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bipartisan bill to streamline permitting for major infrastructure projects could have implications for both housing and energy costs.

Sources indicate that the Senate voted 62-33 to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which would streamline permits and limit the scope of government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and Clean Water Act. Much of that was aimed at massive energy infrastructure, but it also has implications for housing and even data centers.

Senate committee leaders Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), and Mike Lee (R-UT) introduced the bill. It's since been attached to a larger and more popular bill, but lawmakers have been debating and tweaking it for several weeks.

The latest version released this month updated language to assuage concerns that it would weaken environmental protections and rights of Native American groups. The bill has been popular but divisive: While the speed would boost green energy like wind and solar power, plus electric infrastructure that lowers costs, it could also speed along fossil fuel investments, like natural gas pipelines, and nuclear power.

According to recent reports, "Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs," Lee said on the floor before the vote. The bill could make "everything you buy" less expensive in the long run.

According to recent reports, but several housing advocates have cheered the bill, saying it would make it easier to build affordable housing and invest in local communities. They include the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, the Niskanen Center, Associated Builders and Contractors, and the National Community Development Association.

Industry observers note that "America’s housing shortage demands solutions that make it easier and more affordable to build," National Association of Realtors® Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn remarked. NAR "supports streamlining permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction, and limit housing supply.".

Industry observers note that A White House policy paper estimates federal permitting requirements for major infrastructure take 4.2 years to complete—and produce 1,700 pages of paperwork. It expects reforms to increase the GDP by $82 billion to $164 billion and produce $14 billion to $28 billion in tax revenue.

It also mentioned permitting reform could cut electric bills by $178 to $251 a year for the average household. President Donald Trump urged the bill's passage in a post on Truth Social, calling it "a BIG WIN.".

"This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs," the president posted.

"We can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build substantial things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs," Whitehouse remarked.

A number of groups opposed to the bill argued that some of the protections it removes would endanger protections for Native American groups and hamstring environmental preservation.

The Association on American Indian Affairs stated the bill would "threaten Native sovereignty and the protections that safeguard our country's cultural and historic heritage." The Endangered Species Coalition says it would weaken protections. Both continued to oppose the bill even as it was amended.

The House would need to vote on the bill next, and members have already began debating its merits.

According to recent reports, "Even as amended, it undermines Tribal sovereignty, environmental laws, and locks in dangerous projects," Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-NM) stated in an X post. "This is NOT the deal, NOT the time, and NOT what the American people asked for.".

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) cast the bill as a way for Republicans to use the remaining weeks of their majority to improve affordability for Americans.

Recent findings suggest that "One of the biggest things we can do to address affordability for the long term is to ensure a reliable and affordable energy supply," Thune remarked. “And that starts with ensuring that energy projects don’t face unnecessary permitting barriers.".

The federal permitting process, he later mentioned, "has unfortunately gone far beyond these reasonable expectations.

“And that’s due in large part to senseless delays caused by cascading litigation from environmental groups and by agencies determined to study a project to death," Thune mentioned. “We’ve seen those delays happen to everything from water projects to broadband deployment to affordable energy and improving roads and bridges.".

A poll by moderate think tank Third Way found bipartisan support for the tenets of the bill. About 62% of respondents named lowering utility bills as a top concern, and 57% keeping the power grid reliable.

In a recent development, “It’s more important than ever to pass permitting reform this year. The overwhelming support for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act reflects the Senate’s commitment to addressing the nation's energy affordability challenges.".

In a recent development, the bill was also host to Congress' latest effort to rein in data center developments proliferating throughout the country. One amendment by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) would have banned data centers on public lands. Republicans blocked it.

"There is enormous concern that this bill puts the pedal to the floor on data centers across the country," Wyden stated on the floor.

Sources indicate that following Democrats' gains in the House after the 2026 midterms, a number of left-leaning groups have called for a hesitant Congress to formulate more laws involving data centers. Among them, the Chamber of Progress called for federal AI safety standards and requirements for data centers to cover their own costs.

In a recent development, A recent study by the Wharton School indicates that data centers have indeed increased industrial electricity prices in the nation. But it also mentioned that residential customers absorbed relatively little of that price gain.

In a recent development, but that doesn't mean they don't affect communities. A group of Senate Democrats, including Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, released a report pinning other costs on them. It also criticized the tax incentives.

"This investigation finds the data center industry is bulldozing local communities and using their economic resources to play states and local communities against one another, creating a race to the bottom in which state and local policymakers feel they have no choice but to accede to the data centers’ demands—and leaving ordinary citizens stuck with the bills," they mentioned in a joint statement.

In a recent development, voter anger has put data center incentives in the spotlight. Virginia spent over $4 billion in data center incentives over 10 years, according to a state report. Ohio lost $2 billion in foregone revenue from its incentive in two years alone.

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

Florida court tosses Tampa General Hospital's suit against Eli Lilly over 340B discounts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

A Florida federal court has tossed Tampa General Hospital's lawsuit against Eli Lilly over the 340B drug discount program.

According to recent reports, florida's Middle District court dismissed the case on a motion from the drugmaker on Wednesday. If Tampa General Hospital wants to file an amended complaint, it must do so within 30 days.

The hospital initially sued the pharmaceutical firm over a policy it implemented that requires providers to submit claims-level data on pharmacy and medical dispensing if they participate in 340B. Lilly stated it would pull back discounts for providers that did not comply with the requirement and has done so for several organizations, drawing ire from the industry.

Tampa General noted the decision is "unconscionable and immoral" in the initial complaint, filed in July.

In a recent development, however, the district court argued that Supreme Court precedent holds that organizations like hospitals do not have the private right to sue if they have been charged beyond the threshold, based on a 2011 decision. SCOTUS noted that the right to sue was not outlined by Congress, so it is not an avenue available to these organizations.

"The Court made clear that there is simply no private remedy to superintend the pricing and provision of these discounted drugs," per the order.

"To permit this suit would be to encourage piecemeal litigation and defeat the [Supreme] Court’s insistence on maintaining the Congressional plan 'harmoniously and on a uniform, nationwide basis,'" according to the document.

Eli Lilly cheered the decision in a statement.

According to recent reports, "Today’s decision is an vital step toward a more transparent 340B program," a Lilly spokesperson mentioned. "Lilly’s claims data requirement asks hospitals for basic information—information they already give insurers every day—to prevent unlawful duplicate discounts.".

"Decades of HRSA guidance and two federal appeals courts confirm that Lilly can lawfully require this information," the drugmaker said. "More than 3,200 hospitals and clinics already share it with Lilly, and we hope Tampa General Hospital will join them.".

Tampa General Hospital has sued Eli Lilly and Tech giant over the drugmaker’s “unconscionable and immoral” rescindment of discounted pricing under the 340B program.

The complaint, filed last week for the U.S. District Court in the Middle District of Florida, is early legal fallout from a policy Lilly implemented earlier this year that requires providers participating in the federal subsidy program to submit claims-level data for all pharmacy and medical dispensations. The organization threatened to pull the discounts for those that didn’t comply and made good on its threat for a subset of hospitals last month, sparking outrage among provider groups.

Recent findings suggest that tampa General, a nearly 1,000-bed disproportionate share hospital, confirmed in the legal complaint that it was among those cut off. It is now spending 25% to 50% more on average for Lilly products, “many of which it must purchase because of Lilly’s status as the market’s only supplier of a given drug product.”.

In a recent development, tampa General’s lawsuit frequently describes Lilly in such terms, framing the drugmaker as holding significant monopoly power and wielding it in violation of the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. It also often draws contrast to the 340B program’s intent to support the margins of safety-net hospitals providing care to vulnerable patients, against Lilly’s current status as the largest pharmaceutical firm in the world by market cap.

A spokesperson for Lilly, in a statement given to Fierce Healthcare, described the lawsuit as “just another part of the broader hospital campaign to fight transparency and hide the fraud, waste and abuse that plague the 340B program.”.

Tampa General asked the court to order an immediate end to Lilly’s policy and to award damages for the higher prices to which the hospital was subjected. It contends Lilly’s alleged failure to comply with 340B pricing requirements and decision to continue marketing its products as 340B-discounted are unfair trade practices under the Florida statute.

Industry observers note that “The most valuable pharmaceutical firm in the world is engaged in a campaign to transfer dollars earmarked for charitable purposes into its own pocket,” the complaint reads. “The direct and inevitable result of Lilly’s actions is reduced healthcare for poor people. Its actions shock the conscience and are self-evidently unconscionable.”.

Tampa General, similar to the hospital associations that have protested Lilly’s policy, contends that the claims data it requires imposes substantial administrative burden on 340B providers. Even “hospitals who have caved to Lilly’s upcoming demands” have effectively had the prices for their covered outpatient drugs increased due to those administrative costs, it wrote in the complaint.

It has been revealed that lilly and other drugmakers who have signaled similar aims have remarked they need claims data to spot instances in which a drug purchase is improperly granted multiple discounts under overlapping programs. The company has also disputed that the burden of its policy is as substantial as hospitals say.

Industry observers note that “The claims data Lilly requires hospitals to share is information they already collect and send to insurers regularly,” the Lilly spokesperson stated of the lawsuit’s claims. “Refusing to share that same data with Lilly shows that hospitals are more concerned with hiding rampant abuse in the program than improving its integrity. Lilly will keep working to ensure this program serves vulnerable patients instead of hospitals and their for-profit partners.”.

The 340B program has proven to be a magnet for industry and policy conflict, particularly in recent years as its scale has ballooned. The divide is most evident in the ongoing clash over a pilot rebate program that the Trump administration attempted to launch at the top of the year but was forced to restart after the hospital industry’s legal pushback.

340B providers also received a shock this past week when the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services floated a significant reduction in its 340B reimbursement to 33.4% below average sales price in its annual proposed rule on hospital outpatient payments.

Cigna is making $31.5 million in grant funding available over the next three years to nonprofits in 10 states that are aiming to tackle several key community health priorities.

Recent findings suggest that the firm said that funds will be made available through its philanthropic arm, the Cigna Group Foundation, with applications open now through Dec. 18. Cigna said in an announcement that it's looking for organizations tackling youth mental health, veteran wellness and the impact of complex health needs on patients and their caregivers.

Cigna remarked the program seeks to deepen the manufacturer's community health strategy to address critical challenges.

The firm first launched a new approach to community health and engagement in 2024, and since then has deployed more than $30 million in funding to 190 nonprofit organizations. Projects backed by these grants have reached at least 321,000 people, Cigna said.

"Over the past several years, we’ve seen the tangible impact we can make when we invest in strong nonprofit partners and come together to help communities achieve better health and vitality," stated Melissa Skottegaard, board chair of The Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. "We’re building on what’s working, bringing together funding, collaboration and the skills of our employee volunteers to address some of the most pressing health challenges facing communities across the street and around the world.".

Cigna will allot $10.5 million to each of the three focus areas under the initiative, per the announcement. Youth mental health, for example, has been a leading topic at the manufacturer for some time, and the company stated it will also continue to build on its partnership with the Boys and Girls Clubs of America in this area.

It has been revealed that in that partnership, Cigna has helped build out trauma-informed care services to 90% of clubs, reaching 11,000 employees. The tech giant said that these efforts have supported 1,600 youths, and that its workforce has contributed more than 2,000 hours to local clubs.

Eligible organizations can apply for two-year, $250,000 grants to support programs in the three categories. The funds will be available to groups in Arizona, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Missouri, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Texas, per the announcement.

Cigna remarked its foundation will also continue to support community health through its Health Equity Impact Fund.

According to recent reports, "Community organizations can be a powerful source of support for people navigating complex health conditions,” mentioned Matt Perlberg, president of Evernorth Pharmacy & Care Delivery and board member of the Cigna Group Foundation, in the announcement. “By helping patients and caregivers connect with resources and overcome barriers to care, these organizations can provide notable support alongside essential medical treatment, helping people navigate their health and care journey.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.
  • It has been revealed that the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov.
  • Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage rates surged higher this week, reversing four consecutive weeks of declines as persistent inflation and geopolitical worries pushed borrowing costs back up.

It has been revealed that the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% for the week ending Nov. 19, up 17 basis points from 7.11% recorded the week before, according to Freddie Mac.

Borrowing costs also remain substantially above where they stood a year ago, when rates averaged 6.26% during the same period in 2025.

Sources indicate that so what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

Recent findings suggest that at today's 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,354. This reflects a $40 monthly increase from the previous week’s payment of $2,314.

Compared to the 6.26% average from November 2025, which required a $2,120 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $234 more a month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

In a recent development, on a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.28% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,839.

According to recent reports, this reflects a $48 increase from last week's monthly cost of $2,791. Compared to the 6.26% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,558, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $281 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $145 in relief.

The long-term financial picture shows how this abrupt reversal affects total borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.28% rate will pay a total of $847,328 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage.

While this week's jump erased much of the ground gained over the past month, this total still represents a contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630.

By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $43,302 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

Recent findings suggest that FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.28% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,022,090 for principal and interest.

If that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $52,233 for FHA buyers.

Exercise after ACL surgery may protect knees from early osteoarthritis

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but new research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference.
  • Recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected.
  • Recent findings suggest that medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A serious knee injury can cause problems that persist long after surgery, but new research suggests that the right exercise program could make a major difference. A clinical trial led by researchers at La Trobe University found that supervised exercise and education can improve knee health, reduce pain, and enhance quality of life in young adults recovering from anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. The findings also offer hope for addressing their elevated risk of developing knee osteoarthritis at an unusually young age.

Recovery from ACL surgery is often more difficult than expected. About half of patients are still dissatisfied with their knee health two years after the procedure. Even more concerning, roughly half develop signs of early-onset knee osteoarthritis within a decade, often before reaching age 40.

Recent findings suggest that medical guidelines recommend combining exercise rehabilitation with patient education after ACL surgery, yet many people receive treatment that falls short of these recommendations. One obstacle is the widespread concern, shared by some patients and healthcare professionals, that exercise could damage already vulnerable knee cartilage.

A Latest Approach to Recovery After ACL Surgery.

Industry observers note that to investigate whether additional rehabilitation could help, researchers at La Trobe University's Sport and Exercise Medicine Research Centre conducted the SUPER-Knee clinical trial. It was the first study to evaluate the benefits of combining exercise therapy and education more than nine months after ACL reconstruction, a time when patients are generally expected to have recovered even though many continue to experience problems.

The researchers enrolled 184 adults between the ages of 18 and 40 who were still struggling with knee symptoms one to three years after their operations. Participants were assigned to either a progressive exercise therapy program or a comparison group that received a single educational session.

The findings, published in Annals of Internal Medicine, indicated that participants who completed the four-month program under the guidance of a physical therapist experienced improvements in knee health and muscle strength, along with less pain and better quality of life.

Importantly, these benefits came without evidence that the exercises were damaging knee cartilage or worsening early osteoarthritis. The results challenge the belief that physical activity necessarily makes injured knees worse.

Exercise Offers Hope Against Early Knee Osteoarthritis.

Associate Professor Adam Culvenor, who led the research, mentioned the findings provide much-needed evidence about how to help younger patients who remain at risk of knee osteoarthritis following ACL surgery.

"Currently we don't have any high-quality evidence for what treatments should be offered to young people at risk of early-onset knee osteoarthritis. Our SUPER-Knee study changes this, and addresses a globally recognized research priority," Associate Professor Culvenor remarked.

"Our study demonstrated physiotherapist-supervised exercise therapy and education is safe and should be recommended to improve the knee health of young people at high risk of early-onset osteoarthritis following ACL reconstruction.

"The evidence generated by the SUPER-Knee trial can be used to enhancement international clinical practice guidelines for rehabilitation following ACL reconstruction and could be a lifeline for young people struggling after serious knee injuries.

"The intervention is ready to be used by local health professionals with minimal specialized equipment or staff training.".

According to recent reports, the findings could influence how clinicians approach rehabilitation long after ACL surgery, particularly for patients whose symptoms continue beyond the usual recovery period. Although the trial did not establish whether the program prevents osteoarthritis over the long term, it demonstrated that supervised exercise can improve knee health without accelerating the cartilage damage or early osteoarthritis researchers were monitoring.

Years of Knee Pain After a Serious Sports Injury.

In a recent development, for Ruby Cumming, the challenges of recovering from ACL surgery were deeply personal. In 2019, when she was 24, she tore her ACL while playing Australian rules football. Hoping to return to the sport as swiftly as possible, she underwent reconstructive surgery within six weeks.

Recent findings suggest that but the operation did not lead to the recovery she had imagined. Her rehabilitation continued for years, and she ultimately decided not to return to football.

"I thought if I had the surgery and did the rehab I'd be able to get back to normal. After surgery impacted my entire life - not just footy - I changed my outlook and decided I wanted to avoid re-injuring my knee ever again so haven't played contact sport since," Ruby mentioned.

"Experiencing regular pain, not being able to walk, getting public transport to work and living independently all became really challenging for me.".

Cumming remained committed to her rehabilitation, regularly attending physical therapy appointments and performing prescribed exercises. She initially exercised daily before moving to a weekly routine. Despite those efforts, she continued to experience varying degrees of knee pain every day for three to four years.

Her experience changed after she enrolled in the SUPER-Knee trial and began participating in weekly rehabilitation sessions supervised by a physical therapist.

"When I joined the SUPER-Knee program and did weekly physio-supervised rehab, this improved my pain significantly," Ruby mentioned.

The research suggests that people who continue to struggle after ACL reconstruction may benefit from additional structured rehabilitation, even years after their original injury. Because the program requires little specialized equipment or additional staff training, researchers say healthcare professionals could readily incorporate it into existing treatment services.

The SUPER-Knee clinical trial received funding through a Project Grant from Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC).

💡 Key Takeaways
